elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决关于登革病毒在儿童患者中的流行病学特征、分类及临床意义的最新信息缺乏问题,鉴于每年报告的病例数量不断增加。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对当前关于登革病毒在儿科患者中证据的综述,重点探讨流行病学数据、分类标准和临床意义,特别强调与疾病严重形式相关的风险因素。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究对登革病毒的相关现有文献进行了全面回顾,重点关注儿科人群,包括与重症登革热相关的流行病学数据、分类系统和临床结果。
elements_zh.main_results: 证据表明,儿童登革热与因血管通透性、止血、血小板减少和器官损伤等并发症导致的住院风险以及死亡率更高。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为登革热在儿童中的严重程度受到病毒、免疫系统和宿主因素之间复杂相互作用的影响,这是理解儿童登革热结局的一种新颖视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为改善儿童登革热的监测、诊断和预防策略提供信息,特别是在识别重症登革热的风险因素和指导临床管理方面。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于现有文献,可能缺乏近期数据,由于依赖观察性报告而非实验数据,其证据被认为是中等的。

RELEVANCIA: La evidencia sobre la enfermedad del dengue que involucra niños es escasa, con reportes epidemiológicos que datan más de una década; y no describen las implicaciones de las formas graves del virus del dengue en el grupo pediátrico que tienen mayor riesgo de hospitalización por complicaciones relacionadas con alteraciones de la permeabilidad vascular, hemostasia, trombocitopenia entre otras que sugieren daño a órganos diana y choque; es decir, las complejas interacciones entre el virus del dengue, el sistema inmunitario y los factores propios del huésped determinan el nivel de gravedad de la enfermedad en niños y adolescentes con aumento del riesgo de hospitalización y mortalidad.
papers.abstract_zh: 引言:登革病毒是一种由伊蚊属节肢动物传播的虫媒病毒,主要在热带和亚热带地区传播,有4种主要血清型;每年报告的病例数量呈上升趋势。根据世界卫生组织的最新分类,登革病分为有警告症状的登革病和无警告症状的登革病,以及重症登革病。尽管该病可影响任何年龄段的人群,但儿童和青少年更容易发展为重症形式,尤其是那些有合并症的患者。目标:生成一份关于登革病毒在儿科患者中的主要流行病学、分类及临床和预防方面的最新综述。相关性:关于涉及儿童的登革病的证据较为有限,且流行病学报告已有十多年的历史;这些报告并未充分描述登革病毒重症形式在儿科群体中的影响,这些形式与因血管通透性、止血、血小板减少等改变而导致的住院风险增加有关,提示了靶器官损伤和休克的可能;也就是说,登革病毒、免疫系统和宿主自身因素之间的复杂相互作用决定了儿童和青少年登革病的严重程度,增加了住院和死亡的风险。研究问题与背景:本研究旨在解决关于登革病毒在儿科患者中的流行病学特征、分类及临床意义的更新信息缺乏问题,鉴于每年报告的病例数量不断增加。研究设计与人群:本研究是对登革病毒在儿科患者中现有证据的综述,重点在于流行病学数据、分类标准及临床意义,特别强调与重症形式相关的风险因素。方法:本研究对现有文献进行了全面回顾,重点关注儿科人群,包括登革病毒的流行病学数据、分类系统及与登革病毒相关的临床结果。主要结果:证据表明,儿童登革病与因血管通透性、止血、血小板减少及器官损伤等并发症导致的住院率和死亡率增加有关。解释与创新性:作者认为,登革病毒在儿童中的严重程度受到病毒、免疫系统及宿主自身因素之间复杂相互作用的影响,这是理解儿科登革病结果的一个新颖视角。科学与公共卫生意义:这些发现可以用于改善登革病毒在儿童中的诊断、治疗和预防策略,特别是在识别重症疾病的风险因素和指导临床管理方面。局限性与证据强度:本研究基于现有文献,可能缺乏最新的数据,且由于依赖观察性报告而非实验数据,证据被认为是中等强度的。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决关于登革病毒在儿童患者中的流行病学特征、分类及临床意义的最新信息缺乏问题,鉴于每年报告的病例数量不断增加。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对当前关于登革病毒在儿科患者中证据的综述,重点探讨流行病学数据、分类标准和临床意义,特别强调与疾病严重形式相关的风险因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究对登革病毒的相关现有文献进行了全面回顾,重点关注儿科人群,包括与重症登革热相关的流行病学数据、分类系统和临床结果。
analysis_zh.main_results: 证据表明,儿童登革热与因血管通透性、止血、血小板减少和器官损伤等并发症导致的住院风险以及死亡率更高。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为登革热在儿童中的严重程度受到病毒、免疫系统和宿主因素之间复杂相互作用的影响,这是理解儿童登革热结局的一种新颖视角。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为改善儿童登革热的监测、诊断和预防策略提供信息,特别是在识别重症登革热的风险因素和指导临床管理方面。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于现有文献,可能缺乏近期数据,由于依赖观察性报告而非实验数据,其证据被认为是中等的。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Vanuatu Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #16 (Efate, Santo, Tanna and Malekula Island) Format Situation Report Source SPC Posted 17 Nov 2026 Originally published 17 Nov 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 275.68 KB) Suspected case definition: Any person with an acute fever illness that lasts more than 2 days with two or more of the following: anorexia and nausea; aches and pains; rash; low white blood cell count; tourniquet test positive; warning signs Confirmed case definition: A suspected case with laboratory confirmation through: Isolation of dengue virus or detection of dengue-specific antigen or antibodies in tissue, blood, CSF or other body fluid by an advanced laboratory test. Outbreak threshold: Four confirmed dengue cases reported within a single epidemiological week. Circulating serotype: 16 samples were referred for confirmatory testing and serotyping. All 16 samples were confirmed as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) for both Efate and Santo Island. Tanna Island serotype still pending. analysis.time: The report was published on 17 Nov 2026, and the outbreak threshold was defined as four confirmed dengue cases reported within a single epidemiological week.
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers Efate, Santo, Tanna, and Malekula Islands in Vanuatu, with a focus on dengue virus activity in these regions.
analysis.event: A dengue outbreak was reported, with suspected cases defined by acute fever illness lasting more than 2 days and meeting specific clinical criteria, and confirmed cases requiring laboratory testing for dengue virus or specific antigens/antibodies.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Sixteen samples were referred for confirmatory testing and serotyping, with all 16 samples confirmed as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) on Efate and Santo Island. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report outlines the outbreak threshold and case definitions, but no specific details on investigation, testing, isolation, or contact tracing are provided. The status of Tanna Island's serotype remains unresolved.

analysis.brief_en: Vanuatu's Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #16, published on 17 November 2026, details the ongoing dengue situation on Efate, Santo, Tanna, and Malekula Islands. The report defines suspected cases as individuals with acute fever illness lasting more than two days and presenting two or more symptoms such as anorexia, nausea, aches, rash, low white blood cell count, tourniquet test positivity, or warning signs. Confirmed cases require laboratory confirmation through the isolation of dengue virus or detection of dengue-specific antigens or antibodies. Sixteen samples were referred for testing and serotyping, with all 16 samples confirmed as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) on Efate and Santo Island. However, the serotype for Tanna Island is still pending. The outbreak threshold of four confirmed cases within an epidemiological week has been met, indicating a significant public health concern. The report does not provide specific details on investigation, testing, isolation, or contact tracing measures, and the status of Tanna Island remains unresolved.

Sixteen samples were referred for testing and serotyping, with all 16 samples confirmed as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) on Efate and Santo Island. However, the serotype for Tanna Island is still pending. The outbreak threshold of four confirmed cases within an epidemiological week has been met, indicating a significant public health concern. The report does not provide specific details on investigation, testing, isolation, or contact tracing measures, and the status of Tanna Island remains unresolved.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Brazil + 17 more Dengue Epidemiological Situation in the Region of the Americas - Epidemiological Week 42, 2026 Format Situation Report Source PAHO Posted 14 Nov 2026 Originally published 14 Nov 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 928.39 KB) ln the epidemiological week (EW) 42 of 2026, a total of 1,914,591 suspected cases of dengue were reported, resulting in a cumulative incidence of 191 cases por 100,000 population. This represents a decrease of 53% compared to the same period in 2025 and 61 % compared to the average of the las! 5 years. Figure 1 shows the trend of suspected dengue cases as of EW 42. Out of the 1,914,591 reported dengue cases in the Region, 605,321 cases (31%) were laboratory-confirmed, and 4,059 (0.2%) were classified as severe dengue. A total of 655 deaths have been recorded, resulting in a case fatality rate (CFR) of 0.034%. 22 countries and territories within the region reported dengue cases in epidemiological week (EW) 42, accounting for 34,572 new suspected cases. Of these, 96 were classified as severe dengue (0.2%), and 12 deaths reported, yielding a case fatality rate of 0.035%. The distribution of cases by country is detailed in Table 1. Analysis by subregion Central America and Mexico Sub-reglon. A total of 4,837 new suspected dengue cases were registered in EW 42 As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 35% compared to the same week in 2025 and 64% compared to the average of the last five years (Figure 3). The cases reported this week by Costa Rica represent an increase of 41%, México of 39% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Caribbean Sub-region. 215 new suspected dengue cases were registered in EW 42. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 63% compared to the same week in 2025 and 72% compared to the average of the last five years (Figure 4 ). The cases reported this week by Republica Dominicana represent an increase of 57% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Andean Sub-region. ln EW 42, 12,931 new suspected dengue cases were registered. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an increase of 17% compared to the same week in 2025 and a decrease of 5% compared to the average of the las! five years (Figure 5). The cases reported this week by Peru represent an increase of 51%, Colombia of 28%, Ecuador of 12% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Southern Cone Sub-region. 16,589 new suspected dengue cases were reported in EW 42. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 61 % compared to the same week in 2025 and 65% compared to the average of the las! five years (Figure 6). The cases reported this week by Paraguay represent an increase of 39% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Of these, 96 were classified as severe dengue (0.2%), and 12 deaths reported, yielding a case fatality rate of 0.035%. The distribution of cases by country is detailed in Table 1. Analysis by subregion Central America and Mexico Sub-reglon. A total of 4,837 new suspected dengue cases were registered in EW 42 As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 35% compared to the same week in 2025 and 64% compared to the average of the last five years (Figure 3). Caribbean Sub-region. 215 new suspected dengue cases were registered in EW 42. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 63% compared to the same week in 2025 and 72% compared to the average of the last five years (Figure 4 ). The cases reported this week by Republica Dominicana represent an increase of 57% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Andean Sub-region. ln EW 42, 12,931 new suspected dengue cases were registered. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an increase of 17% compared to the same week in 2025 and a decrease of 5% compared to the average of the las! five years (Figure 5). The cases reported this week by Peru represent an increase of 51%, Colombia of 28%, Ecuador of 12% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). Southern Cone Sub-region. 16,589 new suspected dengue cases were reported in EW 42. As of this week, the subregion exhibits an decrease of 61 % compared to the same week in 2025 and 65% compared to the average of the las! five years (Figure 6). The cases reported this week by Paraguay represent an increase of 39% compared to the previous four epidemiological weeks (Figure 2). All new positive cases since 29 October came from Ebeye, the most recent with onset on 09 November, while in Majuro the last confirmed case had onset on 18 October. There have been 18 hospitalisations since the beginning of the outbreak (Majuro 13, Ebeye 5), all children and no deaths. Positivity rates are 26% in Majuro and 35% in Ebeye, and attack rates 5.5 and 4.6 per 1,000 population, respectively. 71% of positive cases are under 20 years of age. Only DENV-1 has been identified. The red alert for dengue (DENV-1) is changed to a blue alert for Marshall Islands. – Source: Republic of the Marshall Islands Ministry of Health and Human Services, Communicable Disease Weekly Report for EpiWeek 45, including the 20th Outbreak Situation Report on dengue fever in Majuro and Ebeye shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 16 November 2026. • Samoa: Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 81 covering EpiWeek 44 (26 October to 1st November 2026) reports 37 new cases, up 3% on the previous week, with one laboratory-confirmed case (in comparaison to two in EpiWeek 43), two new admissions and no death. Since 1st January 2025, 20,553 clinically diagnosed cases, 5,550 laboratory-confirmed cases and nine dengue-related deaths have been recorded. DENV-1 accounts for 52% and DENV-2 for 48% of serotyped cases, and children under 15 years for 73% of cases. The blue alert for dengue (DENV-1 & DENV-2) remains in effect. – Source: Ministry of Health Samoa, Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 81 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 16 November 2026. • Vanuatu: Situation Report #16 on the dengue outbreak reports 259 new laboratory-confirmed cases from EpiWeek 41 to 45 (05 October to 08 November 2026), mostly on Tanna (152) and Santo (76), with 20 on Efate and 17 on Malekula. The cumulative total reaches 476 confirmed cases on four islands: Efate 178, Tanna 167, Santo 100 and Malekula 18. Weekly cases peaked at 109 in EpiWeek 42, driven by Tanna (73 cases), then fell to 41 in EpiWeek 43 and 22 in each of EpiWeeks 44 and 45. Transmission, first concentrated in Shefa Province, increased sharply in Tafea between EpiWeeks 40 and 42. Seventeen dengue-associated hospitalisations have been reported, all discharged, with no severe dengue and no deaths. DENV-1 has been confirmed in 16 samples from Efate and Santo, and serotyping of Tanna samples is pending. The Ministry of Health keeps the outbreak under close observation until a sustained decrease is seen on all affected islands. The red alert for dengue (DENV-1) remains in effect for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Dengue Outbreak on Efate, Santo, Tanna and Malekula Island, Situation Report #16 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 17 November 2026. Diarrhoea • Federated States of Micronesia – Yap State: The Yap weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 45 (02 to 08 November 2026) shows diarrhoea below the alert threshold for a second consecutive week, with 3 cases against 5 in EpiWeek 44 (alert threshold 7), after ten consecutive weeks on alert. One of four stool specimens tested was positive for adenovirus. The blue alert for diarrhoea remains in effect for the Federated States of Micronesia (Yap State). – Source: Yap State Department of Health Services, Communicable Disease Weekly Bulletin shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 13 November 2026. Measles • Australia: On 12 November 2026, NSW Health reported a confirmed measles case in a traveller recently returned from South Asia, where outbreaks are ongoing. While infectious, the person visited several places in Sydney, including Sydney Kingsford Smith International Airport and a healthcare facility. New South Wales has confirmed 58 measles cases since 1st January 2026. In Queensland, one measles notification was recorded in the week starting 02 November 2026, after none in the three previous weeks. Queensland has recorded 18 measles cases in 2026, 13 acquired overseas and 5 locally. Nationally, the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System recorded 125 measles notifications in 2026 as of 17 November 2026, against 181 in 2025. The red alert for measles remains in effect for Australia. – Sources: NSW Health, Measles alert for Sydney, Queensland Health, Notifiable conditions weekly totals and summary information and the National Communicable Disease Surveillance Dashboard (NNDSS) accessed on 17 November 2026. Pertussis/Whooping cough • Vanuatu: Situation Report 7 on the pertussis outbreak in Penama Province reports no new cases on Ambae Island from EpiWeek 43 to 46 (26 October to 15 November 2026). The cumulative total remains 634 cases, of which 7 are laboratory confirmed. The last cases were reported in EpiWeek 41 (7 cases), after the peak of EpiWeeks 36 and 37 (266 and 307 cases). As of EpiWeek 46, five consecutive weeks have passed without a new case, which suggests that transmission may have been interrupted. The outbreak has not yet been declared over. The Ministry of Health may consider doing so once 42 days (two maximum incubation periods) have passed since the onset of the last case. Two cases have been hospitalised since the start of the outbreak, both discharged, and no death has been reported. The red alert for pertussis is changed to a blue alert for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Pertussis Outbreak in Penama Province, Situation Report 07 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 17 November 2026. Respiratory diseases • French Polynesia: In EpiWeek 45 (02 to 08 November 2026), French Polynesia remained in an influenza epidemic phase, with an increase to 111 laboratory-confirmed cases, 79 of them influenza A, and 38 hospitalisations, including four admissions to intensive care. No new death was reported. Since 05 October 2026 (EpiWeek 41), 283 confirmed cases (233 influenza A), 93 hospitalisations, seven intensive care admissions and three deaths have been recorded. These figures are still to be consolidated. Consultations for acute respiratory infection in the sentinel network also increased, while their proportion remained stable and more physicians reported than in the two previous weeks. Adenovirus, metapneumovirus, rhino/enterovirus and parainfluenza 4 were also detected. The influenza vaccination campaign is ongoing. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for French Polynesia. – Source: Agence de régulation de l'action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de Surveillance Sanitaire de Polynésie française n°40 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 17 November 2026. • New Caledonia: On 09 November 2026, the Department of Health and Social Affairs (DASS) declared the end of the influenza epidemic, all clinical and virological indicators having returned to their usual level, with residual low-level circulation. The A(H1N1) epidemic had been declared on 25 September 2026 (EpiWeek 39). After a peak of 151 confirmed cases in EpiWeek 40, cases fell to 2 in EpiWeek 45, and test positivity from 20% in EpiWeek 44 to 5%. Over EpiWeeks 37 to 45, 599 cases were laboratory-confirmed, and A(H1N1) made up 99.3% of the 420 subtyped samples. People aged 65 and over accounted for 36% of cases. Acute respiratory infections represented 1.8% of emergency department presentations in EpiWeek 45, against a peak of 13% in EpiWeek 41, and 29% of presentations for acute respiratory infection during the epidemic led to hospitalisation. The red alert for influenza A is removed for New Caledonia. – Source: Department of Health and Social Affairs (DASS) of New Caledonia, Vigilance DASS bulletin 2026-#12 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 10 November 2026. • New Zealand: The laboratory-based virology weekly report for week 45 (ending 08 November 2026) records 5,960 influenza-positive specimens since 1st January 2026: 5,514 influenza A (963 A(H1N1)pdm09, 877 A(H3N2) and 3,674 not subtyped) and 446 influenza B. This is 138 more than in the week 43 report, indicating that detections are slowing. The acute respiratory illness dashboard published its last weekly update of the season for the week ending 25 October 2026, and the next update is expected on 26 November 2026. The blue alert for influenza A remains in effect for New Zealand. – Source: PHF Science, New Zealand laboratory-based virology weekly report and Respiratory illness dashboard accessed on 17 November 2026. • Tonga: The weekly syndromic surveillance report for EpiWeek 45 (02 to 08 November 2026) shows influenza-like illness falling for a fourth week, from 54 to 49 cases, while severe acute respiratory infections rose from 3 to 9. From 03 August to 08 November 2026, 623 of 835 ILI cases (74.6%) were tested: 270 (43.3%) were positive for influenza A, 6 for influenza B and 31 for RSV. A total of 101 SARI patients have been hospitalised and a fifth death has occurred among SARI cases, up from four reported in EpiWeek 43. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for Tonga. – Source: Tonga Ministry of Health, Weekly Communicable Diseases Syndromic Surveillance shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 12 November 2026. • Vanuatu: The first situation report on the influenza A outbreak in Shefa and Tafea provinces, covering EpiWeeks 30 to 45 (20 July to 08 November 2026), reports 114 laboratory-confirmed influenza A cases out of 232 samples tested. Confirmed cases rose from 2 in EpiWeek 41 to a peak of 40 in EpiWeek 43, then fell to 32 in EpiWeek 44 and 12 in EpiWeek 45. Efate accounts for 98 cases (86%) and Tanna for 16 (14%), where the first cases were detected in EpiWeek 44. Subtyping identified influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 as the circulating strain. Thirty-three confirmed cases have been hospitalised and no death has been reported. Influenza-like illness reached 7,315 cases over the period, 5,943 in Shefa and 1,372 in Tafea, with a peak of 981 in EpiWeek 43 followed by 754 and 533 cases, still above the alert threshold. The outbreak, declared in Shefa in EpiWeek 42 and in Tafea in EpiWeek 44, remains ongoing. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Influenza A Outbreak, Shefa and Tafea Province, Situation Report 01 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 17 November 2026. Rotavirus • Vanuatu: The first joint situation report on the rotavirus outbreak in Tafea and Sanma provinces, covering EpiWeeks 30 to 45 (20 July to 08 November 2026), reports 1,202 cases, of which 12 are laboratory confirmed (3 in Tafea and 9 in Sanma). Tanna accounts for 929 clinically diagnosed cases (78%), Santo for 259 (22%) and Malo for 2. Cases peaked at 251 in EpiWeek 37 and have declined steadily since, to 8 in EpiWeek 45, although sporadic transmission continues. Children under five account for 82% of cases. Tafea has reported 46 hospitalisations and one death since the start of the outbreak, and no patient remains in hospital. The blue alert for rotavirus remains in effect for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Rotavirus Outbreak, Tafea and Sanma Province, Situation Report 01 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 17 November 2026. Other Information: Dengue • American Samoa: On 12 November 2026, the US CDC published in its Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report a review of the dengue outbreak in American Samoa. From June 2025 to August 2026, 1,048 confirmed dengue cases were identified (211 per 10,000 population), 95% locally acquired and 49 travel-associated. A total of 371 patients (35%) were hospitalised and none died. Of the confirmed cases, 78% of cases were under 20 years of age, and incidence was highest among children aged 10 to 14 years (652 per 10,000). Of 146 serotyped cases, 93% were DENV-1 and 7% DENV-2. No travel-associated case was identified after 15 February 2026, and case counts declined from February to August 2026. – Source: US CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, Notes from the Field: Dengue Outbreak, American Samoa, 2025–2026 accessed on 17 November 2026. Hantavirus • Global: On 12 November 2026, the Institut Pasteur published the results of coordinated genomic sequencing of the Andes hantavirus cluster on the MV Hondius expedition cruise (April to May 2026, 13 cases and three deaths), carried out by laboratories in seven countries. The viruses showed low genetic diversity, consistent with a single zoonotic spillover event followed by human-to-human transmission through close and prolonged contact. Eight of ten apparent mutations were sequencing artefacts, and there was no evidence of airborne spread. – Source: Institut Pasteur, Andes hantavirus: characterization of a rare disease cluster by coordinated genomic sequencing, accessed on 17 November 2026. Respiratory diseases • Northern Mariana Islands: The weekly syndromic surveillance report for EpiWeek 44 (1st to 07 November 2026) records 24 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases (22 influenza A, 2 A(H1N1)pdm09), up from 11 in EpiWeek 43, for 427 in 2026. Influenza-like illness rose to 41 cases, 64% above the average of the three previous weeks. Subtyping by the Guam Public Health Laboratory, released on 22 October 2026, identified three A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses. – Source: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Weekly Syndromic Surveillance Report shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 16 November 2026. news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever patient in critical condition; doctor warns of signs of worsening condition. Patients aged 23 and 53 with dengue fever were hospitalized with severely low platelet counts, serious liver damage, and blood clotting disorders. Check Symptoms Báo Đầu tư•14/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 The National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is currently treating several cases of dengue fever, including two female patients aged 23 and 53 who were admitted with severely low platelet counts, liver damage, and warning signs of dangerous complications. The first case involves patient BH (53 years old, Hai Phong ), who was previously completely healthy and had never had Dengue fever. Approximately 5 days before hospitalization, the patient developed a persistent high fever, at times reaching 39-40°C, accompanied by general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain. Doctors warn that the disease can become dangerous even when the patient's fever begins to subside, especially during the period from the 3rd to the 7th day. Despite self-medicating with paracetamol at home, the patient's condition did not improve, so they went to a medical facility for examination and were diagnosed with Dengue virus infection. Test results showed a rapid decrease in platelet count from 38 to 21 G/L, and elevated liver enzymes, forcing doctors to transfer the patient to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases for further treatment. Check Symptoms Here, the patient still had a high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin at the injection site. Notably, tests showed platelet count was only 23 G/L, liver enzyme levels AST was elevated to 1,939 U/L, ALT was 804 U/L, along with a blood clotting disorder. Doctors diagnosed the patient with severe dengue fever, liver damage, and coagulation disorders, requiring close monitoring to detect early risks of bleeding, circulatory problems, and life-threatening complications. Another case involves patient PL (23 years old, Hanoi ), who had no notable underlying medical conditions. Approximately 7 days before being transferred to the hospital, the patient experienced intermittent high fever, sometimes reaching 39°C, accompanied by chills, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and loose stools. After initial treatment at the medical facility, the patient's condition did not improve, while laboratory test results continued to deteriorate, with platelet count dropping to 21 G/L, liver enzymes AST increasing to 1,907 U/L and ALT to 883 U/L. Find Treatments Specifically, the ultrasound results revealed fluid in the abdominal cavity and bilateral pleural spaces, suggesting plasma leakage, one of the dangerous mechanisms of severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can cause decreased circulating volume, hemodynamic instability, and lead to shock if not treated promptly. Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient still had a fever, was very tired, had petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin, and experienced pain in the liver area. Given the severely low platelet count, serious liver damage, and warning signs of complications, the doctors determined that the patient had severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment. Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 16 patients with dengue fever, including some severe cases requiring continuous monitoring to promptly address complications. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes, and can occur at all ages, including young people or those who were previously completely healthy. According to Dr. Phuc, thrombocytopenia is a common symptom in dengue fever patients; however, the severity of the disease cannot be assessed solely based on platelet count. A comprehensive assessment of clinical signs, bleeding status, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and organ damage is necessary. Check Symptoms You may also like In the two recently admitted patients, in addition to severely low platelet counts, they also had very high liver enzyme levels, coagulation disorders, and other warning signs, indicating that the disease had progressed to a serious stage, posing a potential risk of severe bleeding, shock, and multi-organ damage. One of the dangerous characteristics of dengue fever is that the disease can worsen precisely when the patient's fever begins to subside, leading many to become complacent, assuming their health has improved and not continuing close monitoring. Typically, the critical phase occurs between the 3rd and 7th day of the disease's onset, with the risk of plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or damage to organs such as the liver, heart, and nervous system. Find Treatments If plasma leakage progresses rapidly without being detected and treated promptly, the patient may experience decreased circulating volume, hypotension, shock, and multiple organ failure, or even death. Dr. Phuc specifically noted that patients and their families should not assess the severity of dengue fever based solely on body temperature, because the absence or reduction of fever does not necessarily mean the disease has passed the dangerous stage. People with dengue fever should be taken to a medical facility immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, extreme fatigue, lethargy, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, decreased urination, or any unusual changes in consciousness and circulation. During home monitoring, patients need to rest, drink plenty of fluids as directed by healthcare professionals, use fever-reducing medication at the correct dosage, and absolutely avoid self-medicating with aspirin, ibuprofen, or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as these can increase the risk of bleeding. Besides early detection and timely treatment, experts recommend that people proactively prevent the disease by eliminating stagnant water containers, destroying mosquito larvae, using mosquito bite prevention measures, and consulting with healthcare professionals about dengue fever vaccination when appropriate. According to the Ministry of Health , in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, an increase of 26% compared to the same period, with 21 deaths. According to the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), the South currently accounts for 66.8% of the total dengue fever cases nationwide, followed by the Central Highlands at 17.5%, the Central region at 9.8%, and the North at 5.9%. The disease tends to circulate year-round in many localities, with all four dengue virus types (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4) appearing simultaneously. Of these, DENV-1 and DENV-2 are dominant, accounting for approximately 90% of samples; DENV-3 was re-recorded from late 2024 after a period of low detection. Recently, Dong Nai province recorded the deaths of two women, aged 38 and 59, due to dengue shock, one of whom had underlying diabetes. Both self-treated at home and were only hospitalized on the fourth day of their illness in a state of shock, with blood clotting disorders, liver and kidney damage, and damage to multiple organs. You may also like With dengue fever continuing to put pressure on the healthcare system, the availability of a vaccine in Vietnam is seen as a significant step forward, adding another tool to protect public health. Ms. Do Cao Van Anh, a senior advisor at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, stated that the Dengue virus has four serotypes, meaning that individuals who have previously had dengue fever can be reinfected with a different serotype. Some subsequent infections may have a higher risk of severe complications due to antibody-dependent enhancement mechanisms. The availability of the Qdenga vaccine opens up more opportunities for proactive disease prevention, helping to reduce the risk of dengue fever and some of its serious consequences. However, the vaccine has only recently been introduced and is not yet part of the Expanded Immunization Program, while its reach and coverage in the community remain limited. According to Doctor Van Anh, the Qdenga vaccine is licensed in Vietnam for people aged 4 and older, with a two-dose schedule three months apart. Individuals who have or have not had dengue fever can be assessed for vaccination; prior testing for dengue infection is not mandatory. Notably, vaccination decisions must adhere to professional guidelines, especially for individuals with underlying health conditions or specific health issues. Individuals with acute illnesses and high fevers should postpone vaccination until their health stabilizes. For those who have recently recovered from dengue fever, the timing of vaccination should be advised by a doctor; some guidelines recommend waiting about six months after recovery. Women planning to become pregnant should complete vaccination at least one month before their expected pregnancy. news.title_zh: 登革热患者病情危重;医生警告病情恶化的迹象。- Vietnam.vn
news.source_body_en: A news report from Vietnam.vn on November 14, 2026, highlights a dengue fever patient in critical condition, with severe complications such as low platelet counts, liver damage, and coagulation disorders. The patient, BH (53 years old, Hai Phong), developed high fever and other symptoms approximately 5 days before hospitalization. Doctors at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases warned that the disease can worsen even when fever subsides, especially between the 3rd and 7th day of onset. Another patient, PL (23 years old, Hanoi), also showed severe symptoms and was diagnosed with dengue fever. The hospital is treating 16 patients, including severe cases. In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded over 170,000 dengue cases, a 26% increase compared to the same period, with 21 deaths. The South region accounted for 66.8% of cases. The report emphasizes the importance of close monitoring, timely treatment, and avoiding self-medication with NSAIDs. It also highlights the need for proactive prevention measures and vaccination to combat the disease.

news.content_title: American Samoa Dengue Outbreak: CDC Credits Faster Lab Testing but Cannot Show Fewer Cases
news.content: CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) said on November 12 that American Samoa's dengue outbreak produced 1,048 confirmed cases and 371 hospitalizations between June 2025 and August 2026 with no deaths, and that the territory's on-island laboratory confirmed its first cases within days instead of weeks. The report does not test whether that speed reduced cases, and its case count and hospitalization share closely match the territory's 2016 to 2018 outbreak, so residents and health officials still lack evidence that faster confirmation changed outcomes. CDC staff wrote the report with the American Samoa Department of Health (ASDOH). They call it the first dengue outbreak in the territory with the benefit of on-island confirmatory testing, and they conclude that such testing "can be considered as an effective strategy" to confirm infections and guide rapid local vector control. The incidence was 211 per 10,000 residents, based on 2020 census figures. Outbreak Grew From Six Cases to 1,048 Confirmed Across 54 of 76 Villages American Samoa recorded its first positive dengue test of 2025 on June 20. On July 8, the territory declared a public health emergency after six confirmed cases: two acquired locally and four tied to travel to neighboring Samoa, which was fighting a large outbreak of its own. Imported infections dominated early. Of 97 cases in June through August 2025, 38 (39%) were travel-associated. From September 2025 through February 2026, only 11 of 783 cases (1%) were, and no travel-associated case appeared after February 15, 2026. analysis_en.time: The outbreak occurred between June 2025 and August 2026, with the report published on November 12, 2026. The peak incidence was in December 2025, and the busiest day was during that period.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The outbreak took place in American Samoa, affecting 54 of 76 villages. The population was 1,048 confirmed cases, with 814 patients (78%) under 20 years old and 650 (62%) male.
analysis_en.event: An outbreak of dengue virus was reported in American Samoa, with 1,048 confirmed cases and 371 hospitalizations between June 2025 and August 2026. The CDC and American Samoa Department of Health collaborated to confirm cases and implement vector control strategies.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak had an incidence rate of 211 per 10,000 residents, peaking at 652 per 10,000 in ages 10 to 14. The territory's only hospital, LBJ Hospital, had 18 beds occupied by dengue patients on its busiest day, with a median stay of four days. No deaths were reported, and the report does not mention severe dengue or intensive care admissions.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC credits faster on-island lab testing as an effective strategy for confirming infections and guiding rapid vector control. However, the report does not provide evidence that this speed reduced the number of cases. The outbreak response included spraying 97% of reachable households outdoors and 40% indoors, along with clinician training and health alerts. The report notes that the case count and hospitalization share closely match the 2016 to 2018 outbreak, but without a comparison group, it cannot determine the impact of faster testing.

news.title_zh: 美属萨摩亚登革热暴发:CDC称更快的实验室检测有效但无法证明病例减少 - 技术时报
news.source_body_en: In American Samoa, a dengue outbreak between June 2025 and August 2026 resulted in 1,048 confirmed cases and 371 hospitalizations, with no deaths reported. The CDC and American Samoa Department of Health collaborated to confirm cases and implement vector control measures, including on-island testing that reduced confirmation time. However, the report does not provide evidence that faster testing reduced the outbreak's scale. The incidence rate was 211 per 10,000 residents, peaking at 652 per 10,000 among ages 10 to 14. Most cases (95%) were locally acquired, with 814 patients under 20 and 650 male. LBJ Hospital, the territory's only hospital, faced strain with 18 beds occupied by dengue patients on its busiest day, though it had an estimated 110 usable beds. The outbreak response included spraying 97% of reachable households outdoors and 40% indoors, along with clinician training and health alerts. Despite these efforts, the report notes that the case count and hospitalization share closely match the 2016 to 2018 outbreak, but without a comparison group, it cannot determine the impact of faster testing on outcomes.

Yes Not now Full Episodes Podcasts Newsletters Live By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-dengue-fever-as-florida-reports-more-than-500-cases-this-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year Health Updated on Nov 12, 2026 7:57 PM EST — Published on Nov 12, 2026 7:31 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. On Nov. 5, low flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida's Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It's one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country's largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade. READ MORE: Florida's dengue outbreak is largest in continental U.S. in decades Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti, a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae. Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record high number of people infected on Florida's turf: 524. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve. Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida. As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses. The virus is not transmitted person-to-person, and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection. About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito's bite. The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes and muscle, joint and bone pain. About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death. Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches. Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly. Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care. What is the treatment for dengue fever? There is no specific cure or treatment. Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate, and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding. For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient's blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. Can someone develop immunity to dengue? After being infected with a dengue virus, a person's immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses. A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor. "Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first," Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts. Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that's predominantly circulating now "has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes," Miley said. Why are there so many cases in Florida this year? Florida's climate and environment provides ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive. If someone travels to a dengue endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for her life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley. WATCH: Florida has a dengue problem. The solution may be more mosquitoes "When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen," she said. All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases. "Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026," said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson. Does the risk extend beyond Florida? Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito populations, but any state that does could potentially see local transmission of dengue. READ MORE: How climate change will put billions more at risk of mosquito-borne diseases In 2025, CDC data showed locally acquired dengue in Florida, California and Arizona. In August, Virginia health officials reported a locally acquired dengue fever infection. How can people protect themselves and others against dengue? The mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in standing water, so health officials urge people to be vigilant about eliminating it around their homes. "Dump or cover any standing water — especially after each time it rains," Miley said. Florida's Department of Health recommends discarding old tires and drums, emptying and cleaning bird baths or pet water bowls at least once or twice a week and protecting vehicles and boats with tarps so water cannot accumulate. Prevent mosquito bites by using Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellants such as deet and picaridin and covering skin with shoes, socks, and long sleeves and pants. The mosquitoes known to carry dengue are often considered "day biters," Miley said. If you suspect you've been infected with the dengue virus, seek medical attention and avoid exposure to mosquitoes for seven days following symptoms — that's how long a person would be able to infect mosquitoes, enabling them to spread the disease, Miley said. What travelers need to know Chris Pugh Wed, November 18, 2026 at 3:24 PM UTC 1 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Florida's dengue outbreak is still growing as winter travel season approaches. The state has reported 624 locally acquired cases in 2026, including 100 newly reported cases during the first week of November, according to the Florida Department of Health. Most infections have been reported around Tampa Bay. Spectrum News reports Hillsborough County has recorded 468 cases, while neighboring Pinellas County has 109. An expert told the outlet that cooler temperatures could slow mosquitoes, but Florida would need a freeze to kill them. The numbers have climbed dramatically since late September, when Florida had 190 locally acquired cases. Earlier in the summer, the outbreak was already drawing attention as locally acquired infections began spreading. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Dengue is a virus that spreads mainly through the bite of an infected mosquito. About 1 in 4 infected people gets sick, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Symptoms can include fever, headache, nausea and muscle or joint pain. Severe dengue is a medical emergency. For people heading to Florida, prevention starts with avoiding mosquito bites. The CDC recommends using insect repellent, wearing loose-fitting long sleeves and pants, and staying in places with air conditioning or window and door screens. People can also help by dumping standing water around homes, where mosquitoes can lay eggs. Federal guidance recommends regularly emptying containers such as buckets, flower pots and pet dishes. Anyone who develops a fever or other dengue symptoms after visiting an affected area should contact a health care provider and mention their travel history. OffOn Stream on As dengue continues to rise in Florida, some are worried about underreporting of cases At least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in 6 counties. ByMary Kekatos September 30, 2026, 3:00 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google As cases of dengue fever continue to rise in Florida, public health specialists are worried the true number of infections may be greater. For the week ending Sept. 19, at least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in the state, an increase of 38 cases from the week before, according to data from the Florida Department of Health (DOH). Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa, is reporting the highest number of cases at 170 followed by Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas counties, DOH data shows. Related What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports 1st death and cases rise "There's evidence of local transmission of dengue in several counties in Florida," Natalie Dean, an associate professor of biostatistics and informatics at Emory University's Rollins School of Public Health, told ABC News. "Dengue is not endemic to the United States. That means that it doesn't typically cause local transmission." She added, "There can be occasional outbreaks in the U.S. but this one is notable for its size." Last week, DOH reported the state's first death from dengue fever this year but did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. Close-up of a mosquito biting human skin. Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images Three counties -- Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas -- declared local states of emergency last week. These allow local governments to waive normal procedures, access emergency resources and strengthen efforts to control mosquito populations. Pinellas County crews have been going door to door and spraying areas with high mosquito presence, according to local ABC News affiliate WFTS. "I don't recall a [period] of time when it's been this high in such a sort of concentrated area before," Cameron Wolfe, an infectious diseases specialist and a professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine, told ABC News. Wolfe said there may be an underestimate of the true number of cases in Florida. Cases of dengue can be mild, and people may recover on their own or never be tested. Because dengue can resemble a flu-like illness, patients may never suspect the source of their infection. Additionally, he said that reporting of confirmed cases to either local state departments or the CDC can lag. Popular Reads JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions 2 days ago Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat 1 day ago Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Nov 14 "For every case that we know, there's going to be a bunch that we never find out about," Wolfe said. Related Increased risk of dengue virus infections in the US: CDC Dean added that people can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life, but it's usually the second or later infection that is more severe, leading to further underreporting. "I always think of like the top of an iceberg," Dean said. "We're only capturing some of the some of the cases." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) told ABC News in a statement on Tuesday that the agency is "closely tracking dengue activity" and the "unprecedented" number of cases in the Tampa area. The CDC also said they've provided $800,000 in emergency funds to help with the response. "Because the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, Aedes aegypti, are common throughout many areas of the United States, continued local spread of dengue is possible," the CDC statement said. "The best way to prevent dengue is to protect yourself from mosquito bites by using EPA-registered insect repellant, wearing loose fitting clothes, and controlling mosquitoes in and around your home, such as dumping water." Related Dengue fever cases rise to 6,800 in US amid 2 new infections in Los Angeles: CDC Some research has shown that climate change could be expanding the geographic range and severity of dengue fever. Rising global temperature coupled with more rainfall and humidity -- leading to standing water pools that serve as breeding grounds for mosquitoes -- could increase the number of cases. "Global warming and climate change, in fact, leave places like Florida more wet and more capable of housing these mosquito vectors, so I wouldn't be surprised if this becomes a little more of a perpetual thing," Wolfe said. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling by November 15, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Galectin-3 Restricts Dengue Virus Infection Through Envelope Binding and Immune Signaling Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The host protein galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 infection by directly binding to the viral envelope glycoprotein, inhibiting viral entry, and enhancing pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling pathways, according to laboratory and animal findings reported in Virology Journal. Currently, no antiviral therapy is approved for dengue virus, an important pathogen whose pathogenesis remains a major challenge. Galectin-3 is a recognized β-galactoside-binding lectin known to modulate several distinct viral infections, yet its precise mechanistic role in dengue virus infection and disease development had not been previously established. To systematically determine how this lectin influences viral replication, the research team employed a green fluorescent protein-tagged DENV-2 reporter virus across multiple cellular experimental conditions. The investigators evaluated the biological consequences of administering purified recombinant galectin-3, depleting cellular protein levels through targeted knockdown, and increasing cellular protein abundance through experimental overexpression. In addition to assessing replication kinetics, the authors analyzed specific steps in the viral life cycle, focusing on initial viral attachment to host cells and subsequent viral internalization. Initial cellular observations revealed that active DENV-2 infection led to a marked down-regulation of endogenous galectin-3 expression within host cells. When the researchers introduced recombinant galectin-3 into the extracellular environment, the protein caused a dose-dependent reduction in both DENV-2 infectivity and the production of infectious progeny virus. A comparable inhibitory outcome was observed when cells were treated with conditioned medium containing naturally secreted galectin-3, demonstrating that extracellular forms of the lectin exert antiviral activity against the virus. The inhibitory effect of galectin-3 proved to be highly specific and dependent on defined carbohydrate recognition mechanisms. The antiviral restriction exerted by the protein was effectively reversed by the addition of lactose, a known competitive carbohydrate ligand, as well as by the galectin-3-neutralizing monoclonal antibody B2C10. Conversely, neither the control carbohydrate sucrose nor non-specific control immunoglobulin G reversed the observed viral inhibition, confirming that the protective effect relies on specific glycan binding mediated by the lectin. Biochemical and molecular evaluations demonstrated that galectin-3 physically binds the dengue virus envelope glycoprotein, directly hindering both viral attachment and viral internalization into target cells. To clarify the structural basis of this interaction, computational in silico molecular docking was performed against the viral envelope protein. The docking simulations showed that galectin-3 is compatible with engaging both known envelope glycosylation sites, with aggregate computational binding scores favoring interaction at the asparagine-67 (Asn67) glycosylation site. Genetic manipulation of endogenous galectin-3 levels further corroborated its protective role during intracellular infection. Experimental knockdown of endogenous galectin-3 significantly enhanced DENV-2 replication, whereas the overexpression of galectin-3 successfully suppressed viral replication. Concurrently, galectin-3 amplified intracellular NF-κB activation and increased the downstream expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically interleukin-6, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and interleukin-1-beta, notably doing so without altering transcripts for type I interferons. To determine whether these in vitro antiviral mechanisms translate into protection within a living organism, the researchers assessed disease outcomes in neonatal galectin-3 knockout mice inoculated intracerebrally with DENV-2. Mice lacking galectin-3 exhibited significantly earlier mortality, carried elevated viral loads within brain tissues, and suffered more severe neuropathology compared to wild-type control animals. These animal results confirmed that endogenous galectin-3 deficiency substantially worsens disease progression and neuropathology in vivo. Together, these findings indicate that galectin-3 restricts dengue virus serotype 2 by binding envelope glycans to block entry and by promoting NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory responses. Because galectin-3 deficiency exacerbates infection severity in animal models, the study highlights the lectin as a potential host-directed therapeutic target against dengue virus. However, because these evaluations were conducted in cell culture systems and intracerebrally inoculated neonatal mice, further investigation is required before inferring clinical efficacy or therapeutic utility in human dengue patients. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Nov. 13, 2026, 3:46 p.m. ET Hear this story Florida is experiencing its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with 624 locally acquired cases reported this year. Hillsborough County is the epicenter of the outbreak, with 468 confirmed cases and one death. Recent heavy rainfall may increase the mosquito population and lead to a further rise in cases. The historic surge in dengue fever is getting worse. Florida reported 100 more locally acquired cases in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The mosquito-borne disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total for the year to 624 as of Nov. 7, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous record for Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases. The numbers may climb even higher in the weeks ahead after record rainfall left roads flooded, ditches full, and standing water in many Florida yards. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which now has 468 confirmed cases. Nearby Pinellas County is now up to 109 cases. Locally acquired cases have been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to issue a state of local emergency, which expires Nov. 19 unless the county extends it again as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death has been confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has been this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case each of West Nile and Chikungunya was reported last week. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 21 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Columbia Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Sarasota Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas Seminole "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease-capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 13, 12 counties have reported 624 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 524 reported Nov. 6. There have also been nine positive samples of locally acquired West Nile virus and two cases of chikungunya. Dengue: 624 cases 468 in Hillsborough County 109 in Pinellas County 16 in Miami-Dade County 14 in Orange County 6 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 2 in Seminole County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: nine cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (including one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Columbia County 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 2 cases 2 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County Florida health officials have also reported 422 cases of dengue in victims who traveled from a dengue-endemic area within two weeks of onset. Counties reporting international-travel-associated cases were: Alachua, Bay, Brevard (4), Broward (20), Collier (5), Duval (3), Hendry, Hernando, Hillsborough (26), Lake, Lee (19), Manatee (3), Marion (2), Miami-Dade (271), Monroe (3), Orange (8), Osceola (3), Palm Beach (20), Pasco (3), Pinellas (4), Polk (4), Sarasota (2), Seminole (4), St. Johns (4), St. Lucie (8), and Walton. Six cases were reported in non-Florida residents. What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. The whole province has recorded more than 12,200 cases, including 2 deaths. Dengue fever diễn biến phức tạp, treatment pressure in Dak Lak increases. Photo: Ha May On November 18, BS.CKII Hoang Hai Phuc - Director of Dak Lak Provincial Center for Disease Control said that by mid-November, the whole province recorded 201 more cases of Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF), an increase of 88 cases compared to the previous day. During the day, the locality did not record any more deaths. Accumulated from the beginning of the year to now, Dak Lak has recorded 12,286 cases of DHF and 2 deaths in Tan An ward and Quang Phu commune. Notably, on November 13, the whole province recorded 7 new outbreaks, bringing the total number of recorded outbreaks to 494. Through review, there are currently 75 active outbreaks. Epidemic risk assessment shows that many localities are in very high risk groups, including: Krong Pac, Ea Kao, Tan Tien, Ea Tul, Cu M'gar, Ea Drong, Buon Ma Thuot, Tan An, Tan Lap and Hoa Phu. In addition, the high-risk group has 10 localities, including Quang Phu, Buon Ho, Ea Knuech, Krong Nang, Duc Binh, Tam Giang, Ea Wy, Krong Ana, Phu Hoa 1 and Ea Sup. Some other localities are classified into the mid-risk group. The remaining localities are in the low-risk group, with no new cases recorded in the week or only sporadic cases appearing, no active outbreaks and no continuous increase trend. The treatment situation at medical facilities is also noteworthy. According to quick reports from some hospitals and health centers with beds, 165 hospitalizations were diagnosed with DHF and 5 cases were suspected of having the disease. Faced with the diễn biến of the epidemic, the health sector continues to monitor and supervise the disease situation and outbreaks in the area to promptly detect and control the risk of spreading in the community.
