supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever threatens even young, healthy people; prevention measures need to be strengthened. A 24-year-old man with dengue fever had to be placed on a cardiopulmonary bypass machine due to complications including fulminant myocarditis and multiple organ failure, demonstrating the severity of the disease even in young people. Check Symptoms Báo Đầu tư•17/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 With the country recording over 170,000 cases and 21 deaths, experts recommend combining mosquito control, early detection of worsening symptoms, and proactive disease prevention measures. Dengue fever continues to be a complex issue in many localities, with an increasing number of cases and unpredictable complications. Worryingly, the disease can progress rapidly, causing shock, severe bleeding, damage to the heart, liver, and kidneys, and even threatening the lives of previously healthy individuals. The case of a 24-year-old man in Ho Chi Minh City who was recently saved by doctors at Gia Dinh People's Hospital after developing complications from fulminant myocarditis serves as a warning about the dangers of this infectious disease, which is often underestimated in its early stages. Mr. NKL (24 years old, residing in Vung Tau area, Ho Chi Minh City) suddenly developed symptoms of high fever, chest pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. On November 2nd, the patient was taken to Vung Tau General Hospital for emergency treatment in a state of hypotension. Find Treatments In Vietnam, the dengue fever vaccine is licensed for use in people aged 4 years and older, with a two-dose schedule administered three months apart. Recognizing that the patient was exhibiting severe cardiogenic shock and had a high risk of death, the doctors quickly consulted and transferred him to Gia Dinh People's Hospital for further specialized treatment. Here, the patient's condition deteriorated significantly. Blood pressure continued to drop sharply, forcing the resuscitation team to use high doses of vasopressors and inotropic agents to maintain circulation. Echocardiogram results revealed severely impaired myocardial contractility, while laboratory tests showed extensive myocardial damage, along with impaired liver and kidney function. Find Treatments Notably, test results confirmed the patient was positive for the Dengue virus. Doctors diagnosed the patient with cardiogenic shock due to fulminant myocarditis associated with dengue fever, accompanied by multiple organ failure. Faced with imminent death, the resuscitation team decided to deploy VA-ECMO, a cardiopulmonary bypass system, to support circulation and allow the damaged heart muscle and organs time to recover. After a week of intensive treatment, the patient's heart function gradually improved. The patient was weaned off vasopressors, ECMO was discontinued, mobility was restored, and the patient was discharged. According to the patient's treating physician, fulminant myocarditis associated with dengue fever is a particularly dangerous complication with a high risk of death, even in young people without underlying medical conditions. Check Symptoms According to doctors, ECMO does not directly treat the cause of the disease but plays a temporary role in supporting vital functions, giving damaged organs more time to recover. The effectiveness of treatment depends on the timing of intervention, the extent of damage, and the ability to coordinate intensive resuscitation measures. This case demonstrates that dengue fever is not simply a disease causing fever, headache, body aches, or low platelet count. In severe cases, the dengue virus can be associated with multi-organ damage, circulatory disorders, and can push patients into critical condition in a short period of time. You may also like One of the worrying risks is that the disease can worsen during the fever phase, usually about 3-7 days after onset. Patients and their families may mistakenly believe their health is improving, while the body may experience plasma leakage, blood concentration, shock, or other serious complications. Find Treatments Symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, extreme fatigue, restlessness, lethargy, cold extremities, decreased urination, or shortness of breath should be given special attention. If chest pain, shortness of breath, or signs of hypotension occur, the patient needs immediate emergency care to assess the risk of heart damage and circulatory disorders. Not only the elderly, children, or those with underlying health conditions, but even young, healthy people can experience severe complications from dengue fever. Therefore, timely examination and close monitoring of the disease's progression are crucial in reducing the risk of death. Data released by the Department of Disease Prevention, Ministry of Health, at the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 shows that in the first 10 months of the year, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases and 21 deaths. The number of cases increased by about 26% compared to the same period last year, reflecting the increasing pressure on disease prevention and control efforts. Notably, dengue fever is circulating year-round in many localities, with all four types of the Dengue virus coexisting. Weather fluctuations, urbanization, and favorable conditions for mosquito breeding make the disease increasingly difficult to predict. The risk of reinfection also poses a challenge to disease prevention efforts. People who have previously had dengue fever can still be infected with a different type of dengue virus, while some subsequent infections carry a higher risk of more severe symptoms. Check Symptoms Given the complex situation with dengue fever, health experts emphasize the need to shift strongly towards proactive disease prevention, combining control of disease-transmitting mosquitoes, raising community awareness, early detection of cases, and implementing appropriate vaccination programs. In this context, eliminating the breeding grounds of Aedes mosquitoes remains the fundamental solution. People need to regularly clean their homes, cover water containers tightly, remove items that collect water, change the water in flower vases, and cooperate with health authorities in activities to eliminate mosquito larvae and treat outbreaks. In addition, it is necessary to prevent mosquito bites by wearing long clothing, using appropriate mosquito repellent products, installing mosquito nets on windows, and implementing personal protective measures. Mosquitoes that transmit dengue fever are usually most active during the day, so mosquito prevention needs to be maintained regularly. Along with vector control measures, the availability of dengue fever vaccines has added another preventive tool, contributing to a reduction in the risk of illness and hospitalization for those recommended for vaccination. In Vietnam, the dengue fever vaccine is licensed for use in people aged 4 years and older, with a two-dose schedule administered three months apart. This is a live attenuated vaccine, developed to generate an immune response against four types of dengue virus. Ms. Do Cao Van Anh, a senior advisory board expert at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, stated that individuals who have or have not had dengue fever can be assessed for vaccination; prior testing for dengue infection is not mandatory. You may also like Notably, vaccination should be administered according to professional guidelines, especially for individuals with underlying medical conditions or special health circumstances. The vaccine is contraindicated for pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, individuals with significant immunosuppression, and those with a history of severe hypersensitivity reactions to vaccine components or previous doses. Individuals with acute illnesses and high fevers should postpone vaccination until their health stabilizes. For those who have recently recovered from dengue fever, the timing of vaccination should be advised by a doctor; some guidelines recommend waiting about six months after recovery. Women planning to become pregnant should complete vaccination at least one month before their expected pregnancy. In addition, people currently suffering from dengue fever should prioritize treatment and monitoring for warning signs, and should not receive vaccinations during the acute phase of the disease. Vaccination after recovery must be evaluated through a screening examination to ensure safety. However, experts agree that vaccines cannot replace measures to prevent mosquito bites and eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. Dengue fever is not transmitted directly through shaking hands, talking, or hugging, but mainly through Aedes mosquitoes carrying the virus. Therefore, controlling the disease vector remains crucial in epidemic prevention. The health sector recommends that each family spend at least 10 minutes each week checking for and removing stagnant water sources and mosquito larvae inside and outside the house. Easily overlooked places such as flower vases, water cups on altars, plant pot saucers, water containers, or discarded bottles and cans can all become breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In fact, even a very small amount of water remaining in a can lid or forgotten item can create ideal conditions for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Therefore, covering water containers, collecting waste, turning unused items upside down, and proactively preventing mosquito bites should become regular habits. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots by November 16, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A nationwide, population-representative serosurvey conducted across Timor-Leste has revealed that dengue virus transmission is extensive across the country, showing pronounced spatial variation and severe hotspots of infection risk along northern and eastern coastal zones. By combining empirical age-stratified antibody detection with Bayesian sero-catalytic and geostatistical modeling, investigators established that the annual per-capita risk of dengue virus infection for a susceptible individual exceeded five percent across most geographic areas. The findings provide the first high-resolution, nationwide transmission map for the country, demonstrating substantial disease circulation in rural communities that have historically been underrepresented in case-based clinical surveillance records. Dengue virus infection represents a major global health burden across tropical and subtropical environments, producing severe clinical manifestations including dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome alongside extensive asymptomatic or self-limiting illness. In Timor-Leste, routine public health surveillance has historically depended upon case notifications from healthcare facilities, which systematically under-report true infection counts due to uneven healthcare-seeking behaviors, diagnostic barriers, and regional resource disparities. Because previous serological investigations in the country were limited to a single unrepresentative pilot study carried out between late 2018 and early 2019, the comprehensive geographic scope and underlying drivers of dengue transmission across rural and urban districts had remained uncharacterized until now. To evaluate transmission dynamics across diverse administrative landscapes, the investigative team deployed a three-stage cluster sampling design informed by World Health Organization cluster survey guidelines. Fieldwork executed between October 2021 and February 2023 randomly sampled households derived from the 2015 national housing census across 113 enumeration areas proportionate to municipal population sizes. Field teams successfully visited 102 enumeration areas across all thirteen administrative municipalities of Timor-Leste, achieving an enumeration area participation rate of 90.3 percent. Logistical barriers, including severe weather, impassable roads, time constraints, and staff illness, prevented sampling in eleven originally targeted enumeration areas. Discover more Check Symptoms Infectious disease Study Biology Infectious Disease infections The serological dataset ultimately incorporated 4780 individuals residing within 1755 households across the 102 sampled enumeration areas, representing a household participation rate of 67.2 percent and an individual participation rate of 56.7 percent among enumerated occupants. The median participant age was 28 years with an inter-quartile range spanning 13 to 46 years, and female participants accounted for 59.2 percent of the sampled cohort. Demonstrating the representative demographic coverage of the survey across dispersed settlements, 73.0 percent of the participants resided in households classified as rural during the national census. Venous blood samples were collected via phlebotomy from consenting household occupants aged above one year, with target blood volumes stratified between children and adult cohorts. Collected serum specimens were transported under controlled refrigeration to the Laboratorio Nacional de Saude in Dili and evaluated using the commercial Panbio Indirect dengue IgG enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. This diagnostic assay measures human IgG antibodies directed against any dengue virus serotype, functioning as a marker of past lifetime infection rather than acute illness. Testing identified dengue IgG antibodies in 3931 individuals, yielding an overall raw seropositivity rate of 83.1 percent among participants. A small fraction of samples, comprising 57 individuals or 1.2 percent of the total dataset, fell into the manufacturer-defined equivocal index value range between 0.9 and 1.1 and were conservatively categorized as seronegative in the primary analysis. Discover more health Get Health Tips Get Risk Software To translate binary cross-sectional antibody measures into an interpretable metric of exposure, researchers constructed a hierarchical Bayesian catalytic model. Operating under the epidemiological assumption of endemic equilibrium, the catalytic framework leverages participant age as an indicator of cumulative time at risk, parsing age-dependent seroprevalence curves into force-of-infection estimates. The statistical architecture represented force of infection on the logit scale, nesting individual probabilities within households and households within enumeration areas to account explicitly for intra-household clustering effects. In addition, the model directly estimated imperfect diagnostic accuracy, identifying an assay sensitivity of 99 percent and an assay specificity of 98 percent from the empirical data. The sero-catalytic analysis demonstrated intense spatial heterogeneity in transmission intensity across the surveyed enumeration areas, with median force-of-infection values varying by more than fifty-fold across different locales. Estimated median annual force of infection ranged from a low of 0.010, with a 95 percent credible interval spanning 0.005 to 0.018, in enumeration area 10104032 located in Fatubossa within Aileu municipality, to a high of 0.519, with a credible interval spanning 0.295 to 0.816, in enumeration area 40403012 in Goulolo within Bobonaro municipality. Enumeration areas situated in Bobonaro, Dili, Atauro Island, and Baucau exhibited the highest localized transmission metrics, whereas inland mountainous jurisdictions such as Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera consistently demonstrated the lowest transmission values. Discover more Buy Maps Learn Tagalog Explore History Find Treatments Health To investigate the environmental and climatic determinants governing these spatial patterns, the researchers matched the enumeration area force-of-infection estimates with decadal gridded satellite observations spanning 2011 to 2022. Using stochastic partial differential equations within integrated nested Laplace approximations, the team fitted spatial regression models examining multi-year averages of temperature extremes, vapor pressure, accumulated rainfall, elevation, mid-infrared reflectance, and enhanced vegetation index. Spatial regression analysis established that relative humidity exhibited a significant negative association with dengue virus force of infection. Across the joint posterior distributions, the median regression coefficient for relative humidity at minimum temperature was negative 0.96 with a 95 percent credible interval between negative 1.47 and negative 0.39, while relative humidity at maximum temperature yielded a median coefficient of negative 0.65 with a credible interval between negative 1.20 and negative 0.13. By contrast, enhanced vegetation index showed no statistically significant association with transmission intensity. The inverse relationship with relative humidity corresponds with local geographic gradients, where humidity peaks in elevated, cool mountain terrain but drops along warmer, highly populated coastal plains where mosquito proliferation and human biting rates are concentrated. Extrapolating model dynamics across all 2350 enumeration areas in Timor-Leste generated comprehensive nationwide predictions of transmission risk and expected pediatric immunity. The predictive models pinpointed the highest exposure rates along the northern and eastern coastlines, identifying prominent transmission hubs in urban centers such as Dili, Baucau, and Manatuto, as well as on Atauro Island. When aggregated to municipal boundaries, Atauro Island and Dili municipality displayed median predicted annual force-of-infection rates of 0.27 and 0.22, translating to anticipated median seroprevalence proportions at nine years of age of 91 percent and 86 percent, respectively. Municipalities including Lautem, Liquica, and Baucau similarly sustained force-of-infection values exceeding 0.15, corresponding to an expected nine-year-old seroprevalence above 74 percent. Conversely, high-altitude interior regions experienced substantially attenuated transmission intensities, with Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera municipalities presenting median force-of-infection estimates below 0.05 and expected seroprevalence at age nine falling below 36 percent. The stark contrast between coastal lowlands and mountainous interiors underscores the role of local geography in shaping arboviral exposure. Furthermore, the identification of high transmission rates across rural sectors with negligible historic case reporting highlights the degree to which facility-based surveillance fails to detect widespread mild or subclinical infections, particularly where geographic isolation and limited clinical infrastructure restrict access to formal medical evaluations. The authors noted specific methodological limitations inherent to the survey design and historical datasets. Relying on sampling frames derived from the 2015 national housing census meant structural shifts in dwelling occupancy over the intervening six years could have introduced minor sampling discrepancies, though post-independence stabilization has reduced internal displacement. Additionally, assigning infection exposure to a participant’s current residence cannot fully capture infections acquired during travel between enumeration areas, and the time-constant modeling formulation does not estimate seasonal or interannual outbreak surges. Gridded environmental variables derived at spatial scales between one and five kilometers also necessitated spatial averaging across smaller enumeration areas. Despite these analytical caveats, the nationwide serosurvey establishes an essential baseline for contemporary public health decision-making in Timor-Leste. The reconstructed seroprevalence metrics at nine years of age provide specific empirical parameters mandated by World Health Organization frameworks to evaluate the programmatic introduction of dengue vaccines, such as TAK-003. Furthermore, the high-resolution mapping of transmission hotspots offers operational guidance for mosquito abatement initiatives and the targeted deployment of Wolbachia-infected mosquito release programs, ensuring vector control resources are directed toward communities bearing the highest cumulative infection burden. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Dimer Epitope Antibodies Link to Protection From Severe Secondary Infection by November 14, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dengue Dimer Epitope Antibodies Link to Protection From Severe Secondary Infection Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Antibodies targeting quaternary epitopes across the envelope protein dimer interface correlate with protection against severe dengue disease in patients undergoing secondary dengue virus infection, according to findings from clinical cohorts in Cambodia and Colombia. In contrast, antibodies directed against the conserved envelope fusion loop were found at significantly elevated proportions in hospitalized patients compared with individuals who experienced subclinical infections. Functionally, purified human antibody fractions directed against the soluble envelope dimer demonstrated potent virus neutralization and cross-neutralization against distinct serotypes while exhibiting limited enhancement of cellular infection. Conversely, antibodies recognizing the fusion loop mediated weak neutralization and pronounced antibody-dependent enhancement in Fc-receptor-bearing cells in vitro, clarifying how distinct antibody subsets directed toward the same viral surface protein can drive divergent clinical trajectories during natural post-primary dengue virus exposure. The dengue virus envelope glycoprotein is the primary target of human humoral immunity and is organized on mature virions into ninety homodimers arranged in an antiparallel head-to-tail lattice. Each monomeric envelope subunit comprises three structural regions designated domain one, domain two, and domain three, which together mediate cell attachment and acid-triggered membrane fusion. Within domain two, a hydrophobic fusion loop sequence remains highly conserved across all four dengue virus serotypes as well as related flaviviruses, yet its accessibility on mature virions is structurally constrained beneath neighboring envelope subunits. At the contact boundary formed between two paired envelope monomers, virus assembly generates a quaternary conformational target known as the envelope dimer epitope. While monoclonal antibodies against these respective sites have previously shown differing neutralization profiles in cell culture and animal models, their relative prevalence and direct association with human clinical severity across natural post-primary infections have historically remained unresolved. To investigate these epitope-specific antibody dynamics during active illness, investigators analyzed longitudinal plasma samples collected from children recruited into the prospective DENTHOM project across Kampong Thom and Siem Reap provinces in Cambodia. Patients admitted to Kampong Thom Provincial Hospital, Baray District Hospital, Stuong District Hospital, and Jayavarman VII Hospital with acute febrile illness were confirmed for secondary dengue virus serotype two infection using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction alongside hemagglutination inhibition assays. Hospitalized cases were clinically classified according to World Health Organization criteria into classic dengue fever or severe manifestations comprising dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. Concurrently, household contact investigations surrounding laboratory-confirmed index cases identified infected individuals who developed subclinical infections, defined by absent or mild fever not exceeding thirty-eight degrees Celsius for at most two consecutive days and no more than one accompanying symptom such as rash, nausea, or aches. Using a multiplex microsphere-based immunoassay, the team tracked antibody binding against recombinant soluble envelope monomers, envelope domain three, and engineered soluble envelope dimers produced in Drosophila S2 cells harboring cysteine substitutions at residues leucine 107 and alanine 313. These engineered disulfide bonds preserve the envelope dimer conformation and prevent exposure of the internal fusion loop. By comparing untreated plasma binding against binding following competitive blockade with the pan-flavivirus monoclonal antibody clone 4G2, researchers quantified the exact proportions of fusion loop-targeting antibodies and dimer-specific quaternary antibodies throughout the acute, critical, early recovery, and late recovery phases. Across all post-primary infection phases, antibody concentrations recognizing domain three remained substantially lower than antibodies binding soluble envelope monomers and total soluble envelope dimers, demonstrating that domain three contributes only a modest share of the circulating polyclonal response in naturally infected pediatric patients. Epitope-specific antibody levels exhibited substantial inter-individual variability during early symptomatic presentation but increased markedly over time, reaching peak titers across the critical and early convalescent stages between four and fourteen days following symptom onset. During the acute phase spanning the initial three days of illness, detectable levels of dimer-specific antibodies were present in similar frequencies between subclinical and hospitalized individuals, and no differences in antibody proportions emerged when hospitalized patients were stratified by clinical severity. However, substantial divergence developed during the critical phase four to six days post-onset, which coincides with active viremia and the potential development of plasma leakage. Hospitalized patients showed significantly higher proportions of fusion loop-directed antibodies than individuals with subclinical infection, indicating that elevated proportions of poorly neutralizing, cross-reactive fusion loop antibodies in the critical window correlate with greater disease susceptibility. Among hospitalized children evaluated during the critical phase, the proportion of envelope dimer-specific antibodies proved significantly lower in severe dengue cases with hemorrhagic fever or shock syndrome than in children presenting with uncomplicated dengue fever. Median dimer-specific antibody proportions measured zero point twelve in severe cases compared with zero point thirty-seven in dengue fever, demonstrating a statistically significant protective association. To evaluate whether this immunological pattern extended across different viral serotypes and distinct host populations, the researchers examined an independent adult validation cohort from Cali and Bucaramanga, Colombia, comprising patients undergoing secondary dengue virus serotype one infection diagnosed by multiplex reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and high-avidity immunoglobulin G enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. In the Colombian cohort, hospitalized patients with classic dengue similarly exhibited higher median proportions of serotype one dimer-specific antibodies than those who progressed to severe disease, reinforcing the protective association across geographically distinct populations. To establish the mechanistic properties of these antibody populations directly from patient circulation rather than synthetic monoclonal surrogates, the investigators isolated total polyclonal immunoglobulin G from twelve Cambodian pediatric patients sampled during the critical phase. Utilizing sequential resin affinity chromatography coupled with site-specifically biotinylated recombinant envelope antigens, the authors successfully fractionated domain three antibodies, envelope dimer-specific antibodies, and fusion loop-reactive antibodies. Subsequent immunoassay binding validation confirmed that the dimer-specific fraction selectively recognized envelope dimers without cross-reacting with domain three, whereas the isolated fusion loop fraction bound preferentially to soluble monomeric envelope proteins displaying the exposed fusion motif while showing minimal reactivity against stabilized dimers or isolated domain three proteins. Functional evaluation using flow cytometry neutralization assays in Vero CCL-81 cells revealed that the purified envelope dimer-specific fraction possessed markedly superior neutralizing potency against dengue virus serotype two compared with fusion loop-binding antibodies. Dimer-specific antibodies achieved fifty percent viral neutralization at a median concentration of fifty-five point six nanograms per milliliter, whereas fusion loop antibodies required a significantly higher median concentration of one hundred forty-seven point four nanograms per milliliter to reach equivalent inhibition. Conversely, selective depletion of domain three, monomeric soluble envelope, and envelope dimer antibodies completely eliminated neutralization capacity while retaining residual infection enhancement, an effect likely maintained by non-neutralizing antibodies targeting structural pre-membrane proteins that remain on partially mature virus particles. Infection enhancement assays performed using engineered U937 monocyte cell lines expressing Fc-gamma receptors one, two-a, two-b, and three demonstrated that fusion loop antibodies generated substantially higher rates of antibody-dependent enhancement than dimer-specific or domain three fractions. At a test concentration of three hundred nanograms per milliliter, fusion loop-targeting antibodies induced productive infection in thirty point five percent of cells, compared with sixteen point three percent for domain three antibodies and fourteen point four percent for envelope dimer-specific antibodies. Even when normalized to their respective fifty percent inhibitory concentrations, fusion loop antibodies provoked over thirty percent cellular infection enhancement, roughly double the enhancement frequency observed for dimer-specific antibodies, confirming that fusion loop-directed antibodies display intrinsically heightened enhancing capacity under equivalent neutralization thresholds. Cross-neutralization experiments further underscored the distinct functional utility of envelope dimer antibodies when challenged with heterologous viral serotypes. When tested against dengue virus serotype one, dimer-specific antibodies isolated from serotype two-infected donors demonstrated potent cross-protective efficacy, achieving fifty percent inhibition at a median concentration of two point eighty-three nanograms per milliliter. In contrast, domain three fractions required a median of eighty-two point twenty-nine nanograms per milliliter, and fusion loop antibodies required four hundred eighty-one point one nanograms per milliliter to achieve fifty percent neutralization. These data confirm that while domain three-specific antibodies remain predominantly homotypic, human antibodies directed against the quaternary dimer interface mediate potent cross-serotype neutralization across genetically divergent dengue lineages. The study notes several methodological constraints and biological limitations that contextualize these immunological findings. Competitive blockade relied on mouse monoclonal antibody 4G2 to define fusion loop specificity, which might fail to detect human antibodies binding adjacent overlapping contacts or underestimate high-affinity human antibodies that outcompete the blocking clone. Furthermore, in vitro neutralization assays utilized virus stocks propagated in C6/36 mosquito cell lines, which harbor variable mixtures of immature and partially mature virions whose exposed structural surfaces can alter epitope accessibility compared with fully mature virus structures encountered in vivo. Clinically, determination of past dengue exposure relied on hemagglutination inhibition and antibody avidity assays, which cannot distinguish whether an individual has experienced exactly one prior infection or multiple tertiary and quaternary exposures that naturally skew antibody repertoires toward broader neutralizing profiles. Despite these considerations, the findings establish that the epitope specificity of the polyclonal envelope antibody repertoire represents a pivotal correlate of human dengue infection outcome. The data indicate that high relative proportions of fusion loop antibodies during the critical phase associate with symptomatic progression and hospitalization through Fc-mediated enhancement, whereas abundant quaternary dimer-targeting antibodies reduce disease severity and confer broad cross-neutralizing coverage. These observations offer direct immunological targets for vaccine design, indicating that next-generation immunization platforms should aim to present conformationally intact envelope dimers that elicit protective quaternary responses while minimizing the presentation of accessible, enhancement-prone fusion loop structures. supplementary_news.content: Featured Columns about 2 months ago The Clean Bite: Making Dental Infection Control Part of Every Day about 2 months ago Pathogen Pulse: The Alarming Rise of Dengue in Florida 3 months ago Bug of the Month: You Never See Me Coming Shorts Podcasts Sterile Processing Burnout and Cognitive Overload: How Interruptions, IFUs, and Human Factors Affect Patient Safety Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. From “Gotcha” to Coaching: Using RTLS to Improve Hand Hygiene In this podcast with ICT, Danielle Updegraff, MBA, BSN, RN, discusses real-time location systems, which can give infection prevention teams greater visibility into hand hygiene, workflow, and infectious disease exposures, but sustainable improvement still depends on staff engagement, leadership, education, and culture. AIDS 2026: Malawi Program Achieves 10-fold Reduction in HIV Positivity Among Exposed Infants In this complete interview, ICT speaks with Endale Tilahun, MD, MPH, about a Malawi community program that reduced missed HIV testing and achieved 0.2% positivity among exposed infants through household follow-up, individualized case management, and coordinated health and social support. Experts Call for Standardized Cleaning of Reusable Lead Aprons Environmental testing found bacterial contamination on many lead garments and described what lead garment cleaning technicians routinely encounter during servicing. AIDS 2026 Research Shows Individualized HIV Treatment Is Shaping the Future New research presented at AIDS 2026 indicates that 2-drug HIV regimens and long-acting injectable therapies are effective treatment options that also enhance personalized care. Investigators highlight that shared decision-making, adherence, quality of life, and minimizing long-term medication exposure are becoming more vital alongside maintaining viral suppression. Contagious Conversations: Global Infection Prevention Leaders Say the Future of IPC Depends on Diverse Career Pathways International infection prevention leaders discuss how Ireland and Saudi Arabia educate, recruit, and prepare IPC professionals while advocating for broader, multidisciplinary career pathways worldwide. Hantavirus: A Podcast With an Infectious Disease Doctor A hantavirus outbreak linked to a South American cruise ship is drawing global attention, but experts say fears of a COVID-19-style pandemic are largely unsupported. Infectious disease physician Matthew Pullen, MD, discusses Andes virus transmission, misinformation, cruise ship risks, and what health care professionals should really be watching for. Contagious Conversations: SoCal SPA Chapter Conference Highlights How Voice, Mentorship, and Everyday Practice Drive Leadership and Patient Safety The cohosts of Contagious Conversation speak with Tori Whitacre Martonicz, lead editor of Infection Control Today, about her presentation at the SoCal SPA Spring Conference, and how the conference speakers emphasized leadership beyond titles, urging SPD professionals to share knowledge, speak up, and turn everyday insights into safer patient care practices. The Invisible Heroes: Why Dental Assistant Recognition Week Matters (Podcast) Dental assistants manage sterilization, infection control, and patient education—yet most states require zero formal training. They earn the lowest wages in dental offices. Meet Sherrie Busby's 42-year mission to secure standardized credentialing and fair recognition. (Audio podcast) ICTalk Podcast: 2025 APIC President Carol McLay, DrPH, Reflects on Advocacy, Global Collaboration, and the Future of Infection Prevention As her 2025 APIC presidency concludes, Carol McLay, DrPH, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, FSHEA, discusses public health funding cuts, science advocacy, global partnerships, workforce development, and why infection preventionists must speak up. In this exclusive ICT interview, she shares lessons from a tumultuous year and her vision for strengthening the infection prevention profession worldwide. All News What happens to a towel between uses? Natasha Terborg traces the laundry process from collection to storage and explains which practices from health care guidance can inform everyday laundry in shared facilities. An infection preventionist examines the DRC’s Ebola response through contact tracing and community engagement, explaining why daily follow-up, timely investigations, and trust reveal challenges that cumulative case counts alone cannot capture. Four vaccine experts discuss how sustained financing, local research leadership, and community trust can strengthen vaccine development in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), drawing on practical insights from India and Bangladesh. GeoVax CEO David Dodd discusses how vaccine storage requirements, supplier diversification, and regional manufacturing shape outbreak preparedness, with considerations for infection preventionists and health systems preparing to receive and administer doses. Part 4 of 4: Why better planning for surgical growth, operational performance, and patient safety requires sterile processing expertise early in the decision-making process. An emerging cause of sexually transmitted ringworm, TMVII can resemble other skin conditions and require prolonged treatment. Learn what clinicians and infection preventionists should know about recognition, specialized testing, and patient counseling. The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: Human Plus Machine 3 of 4: How technology, artificial intelligence, automation, and data are reshaping sterile processing leadership The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: Building the Workforce of the Future Part 2 of 4: Recruitment may bring people into sterile processing. Development is what determines whether they stay. At IDWeek 2026, Rachel Sidebottom discusses research exploring phage-antibiotic combinations, the potential for predictive modeling, and an investigation identifying an ST5 strain of nontoxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae circulating in Albuquerque. Finding infections earlier is only part of the work. At IDWeek 2026, David Weber, MD, MPH, explored how broader surveillance and emerging technologies could help infection preventionists spend more time supporting safer care. Two experts give an update ahead of the first season with a new mRNA vaccine against flu. The Next Generation of SPD Leadership: People First, Standards Always Part 1 of 4: How emerging sterile processing leaders are redefining leadership through trust, accountability, psychological safety, and professional development. This week in infection prevention: Kenya’s Bundibugyo virus response shows why execution, not just planning, determines outcomes, and France reported the first known human Shamonda virus infection. Our roundup also covers brucellosis, blood donor screening, and long-acting HIV antibody findings from IDWeek 2026. At IDWeek 2026, Jimmy Chang, PhD, discussed investigational HIV antibodies TMB-365 and TMB-380, explaining their complementary mechanisms, early study findings, and ongoing evaluation as a long-acting maintenance regimen. At IDWeek 2026, Samuel Ntow, MBChB, MPH, discussed research findings of reactive infection screening markers in 18.3% of replacement donor records from rural Ghana, highlighting opportunities for further evaluation and linkage to care. France’s first reported human Shamonda virus infection raises questions about transmission and vulnerable patients. Explore what investigators know, what remains uncertain, and why infection preventionists should follow this emerging story. John Rex, MD, CMO of F2G, discusses investigational olorofim’s phase 3 findings, why new antifungals are difficult to develop, and how an oral option could help patients with limited treatment choices. An analysis of 147 million US hospital admissions identified 875 adults with brucellosis diagnoses, highlighting demographic and regional differences while emphasizing exposure histories and uncertainty about underdiagnosis. Kenya’s secondary Ebola cases raise urgent questions about hospital readiness. Explore what the response reveals about contact tracing, health care worker protection, and the implementation of infection prevention plans. An ICU study found that alcohol-based hand rub applied after patient care reduced glove bioburden, while staff raised feasibility concerns. Researchers stress that the practice does not replace glove changes or hand hygiene. A study of 4,851 nursing home residents linked shared rooms to higher odds of matching MDRO carriage, while universal decolonization was associated with lower concordant carriage across MRSA, ESBL, and VRE. A retrospective hospital study found no significant differences in mortality or readmissions between infectious disease e-consults and in-person consultations, despite more diagnoses of bacteremia among e-consult patients. Researchers recommend further evaluation across settings. Presented at IDWeek 2026, a living review of 64 studies found the strongest evidence for dengue prevention from mosquito modification, while highlighting substantial uncertainty and research gaps in other approaches to Aedes vector control. A 2026 IDWeek poster details how respiratory cultures and whole genome sequencing clarified a NICU MRSA outbreak, with targeted prevention measures followed by at least 6 months without additional bacteremias or related respiratory clusters. Researchers recovered a carbapenemase-producing organism from the shaft of a hospital drain auger, prompting calls for standardized reprocessing protocols and further investigation into maintenance equipment as a potential source of environmental dissemination. A poster presented at IDWeek was a systematic review of 35 studies that found rare transmission of viral hemorrhagic fever to health care personnel in high-income countries and highlighted the need for standardized exposure definitions to guide response. Kimberley Brown, PharmD, Head of U.S. Medical Affairs at ViiV Healthcare discusses the evolution of HIV care and how innovative long-acting injectables are expanding options across HIV treatment and prevention. Clean Hospitals President Alexandra Peters, PhD, explains how training, meaningful support, and stronger collaboration with infection prevention teams can empower environmental services staff and strengthen patient safety. A proposed hepatitis B vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau raises concerns about delaying newborn protection. This commentary examines the ethical obligations of researchers and the consequences of weakening established prevention efforts. For International Infection Prevention Week, Infection Control Today explores how prevention connects hospital departments with everyday community life and why infection preventionists (IPs), sterile processing department (SPD), professionals, and environmental services (EVS) teams deserve lasting support. This week in infection prevention: Kenya's imported Ebola case showed how fever screening can miss an ill traveler, Florida's dengue outbreak reached 296 local cases, and new guidance underscores that missed surfaces and shared equipment fuel AMR risk. Our weekly roundup covers these stories and more. During Sterile Processing Week, Infection Control Today honors the professionals behind safe instrument reprocessing and calls for year-round investment in education, staffing, resources, and meaningful collaboration across health care teams. In honor of Global Handwashing Day, Jamar Shaw, MD, MPH, CIC, explains how applying the WHO 5 Moments to actual care sequences can reduce transmission risks in ambulatory settings

By Research Matters Staff Writer(s) · November 13, 2026 ·Delhi · 4 min read EN Listen Add Research Matters as a Preferred Source on Google Denue testing (representative image Gubbi Labs) New study shows how a molecular chain reaction inside human blood explains why a routine mosquito-borne infection can rapidly turn life-threatening. By analysing the genetic activity of dengue patients at the earliest stages of illness, researchers from the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology, Ashoka University, the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), and Max Super Speciality Hospital in New Delhi found that the most severe cases occur because the initial antiviral defences of the body's immune system are suppressed. This early immune silence allows the virus to flourish unchecked, triggering a dangerous cascade that destroys blood platelets and causes vital blood vessels to leak. Dengue virus infects an estimated 390 million people worldwide each year, with India alone carrying roughly one-third of the global burden. Transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the infection often leads to sudden fever, severe headaches, and muscle pain. For most, the illness resolves within a week. However, a vulnerable fraction of patients suddenly deteriorate, experiencing plummeting platelet counts and plasma leaking out of their circulatory system into surrounding body cavities. Because this collapse can happen without clear warning, identifying which patients will develop severe complications has been one of the challenges facing doctors in tropical emergency rooms. To find an early marker, the research team examined 112 patients who arrived at the hospital during the acute phase of dengue infection. They extracted total ribonucleic acid (RNA) from each patient's blood to observe which genes were actively switched on or off. They then applied an analytical technique called weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Much like mapping a complex social network, this method groups thousands of interacting genes into collaborative modules, allowing scientists to see how broad biological networks coordinate their behaviour in response to disease. Scientists long suspected that severe illness was primarily driven by a massive, hyperactive inflammatory storm. In contrast, the new findings show that patients showing clinical warning signs and dangerous platelet loss exhibited a severely depressed innate immune state. Crucial chemical alarms known as cytokines, including molecules named CXCL8 and interleukin-1 beta, were significantly turned down rather than up. The subdued state causes the body's early interferon security alarm to fail and not mobilise frontline defences. Without resistance, the dengue virus multiplies rapidly and places enormous stress on the circulatory system. This viral surge triggers a secondary crisis within the vascular network. As platelets are cleared from the bloodstream in huge numbers, the physical integrity of the blood vessels breaks down. The researchers discovered that this vascular leakage is driven by non-inflammatory damage to the endothelial glycocalyx, a thin, sugary protective gel that coats the inner walls of our blood vessels. In severe patients, genes responsible for sugar modifications, known as O-linked glycosylation, were heavily overactive, while structural maintenance genes such as cortactin, or CTTN, were downregulated. This molecular disruption strips away the protective barrier of blood vessel linings, allowing fluids to escape into surrounding tissues independently of traditional swelling or fever mechanisms. The study also pinpointed several genes that could serve as early warning clues for hospital wards. A gene called IFI44L, which regulates interferon signalling, showed a dramatic shift in activity between patients with moderately low platelets and those whose counts crashed below critical safety thresholds. Simultaneously, the structural gene CTTN demonstrated the strongest mathematical correlation with falling platelets, serving as a direct window into blood vessel fragility. This research also bridges international observations, corroborating findings from clinical studies in Brazil regarding interferon genes while pinpointing unique blood-vessel maintenance signatures relevant to populations in South Asia. The researchers, however, acknowledged that the investigation was cross-sectional, capturing a snapshot of patient blood at a single moment during early infection. As a result, the study could not track the dynamic rise and fall of these genetic signals through patient recovery, highlighting the need for future longitudinal studies. By identifying the exact genes that signal early disease escalation, clinicians could detect severe dengue days before clinical warning signs appear. Understanding that plasma leakage is linked to the destruction of the blood vessel's sugar coating could also open up entirely new avenues for drug development. In countries where hospital wards are regularly overwhelmed by seasonal epidemics, these molecular insights could save critical healthcare resources and ultimately prevent escalations. The descriptive epidemiological analysis evaluated records compiled from August 2024 through July 2025, providing an overview of outbreak distribution amid widespread instability. The investigation utilized national surveillance data collected over the twelve-month monitoring window to assess the extent of disease transmission. Researchers processed key public health metrics, specifically calculating state-level case counts, associated fatalities, and counts of internally displaced persons using R software version 4.2.2. Geographic analysis revealed marked variations in disease burden across the ten affected states, with the conflict-affected region of Khartoum State recording the highest overall volume of infections. Surveillance figures indicated that Khartoum accounted for 8,040 of the total reported cases during the observation period. While Khartoum experienced the largest aggregate case tally, Kassala State recorded nine deaths, the highest number of fatalities among the reporting states. Kassala also documented the largest concentration of dengue infections among internally displaced persons, registering 472 cases within displaced populations. In contrast to the high displacement-associated case burden observed in Kassala State, Khartoum State documented 69 dengue cases among internally displaced persons. The collected surveillance variables across all ten states tracked these disparate intersections between displacement figures, regional transmission counts, and overall mortality outcomes. Based on the surveillance data, the study authors emphasized that strengthened dengue surveillance and vector control interventions are urgently needed in conflict-affected settings. The researchers observed that disruptions to essential health services in these environments create substantial challenges for outbreak prevention and effective public health response. Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield breaks down the risks of transmission and essential prevention measures. Meanwhile, Hillsborough County mosquito management teams deploy aerial spraying to target the mosquitoes carrying the virus. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! You probably aren't thinking much about mosquitoes in November. In much of the country, cooler weather has sent those annoying little bloodsuckers into hiding. But in Florida, mosquitoes are still causing serious trouble. The state is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades, and hundreds of people have caught the virus without leaving the state. Now, researchers at the University of South Florida have developed an AI mosquito trap that could help health officials find dangerous mosquito species much faster. It can identify mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. And with dengue still spreading in Florida, the timing couldn't be more important. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE The Digitomy AI mosquito trap uses built-in cameras and artificial intelligence to identify mosquito species that can spread diseases like dengue. (University of South Florida) Why Florida's dengue outbreak is making headlines now If you thought mosquito season ended when summer did, Florida has a different story to tell. According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County has recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, the county's largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, health officials have reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. That means people contracted the virus from mosquitoes in the area rather than while traveling overseas. The Tampa area has been hit especially hard. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain. In serious cases, it can lead to life-threatening complications. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. On November 13, Hillsborough County announced that it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments to help contain the outbreak. County officials say mosquito surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area. And here's why we're talking about this in November. While mosquitoes have largely disappeared from colder parts of the country, they can remain active in warmer states. Florida's outbreak shows that the threat doesn't disappear simply because summer is over. Meanwhile, a new generation of technology could give communities a better way to respond before mosquito populations get out of control. How the new AI mosquito trap works The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by researchers at the University of South Florida. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have been developing the system through research dating back to 2018. Their goal is to help mosquito control teams identify the insects they're catching without spending days examining them under a microscope. The trap itself looks fairly straightforward. Workers can hang it from a low tree branch or place it on the ground. A light or bait attracts mosquitoes, and a small fan pulls them inside. Once the insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. Artificial intelligence then compares those images against a large database to determine which mosquito species have been captured. But the technology goes further. It can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. That's useful information because female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. The researchers say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing. GOOGLE WANTS TO RELEASE MILLIONS OF MOSQUITOES A researcher displays mosquitoes collected by the smart trap, which uses AI to identify potentially dangerous species much faster than traditional methods. (University of South Florida) Why identifying mosquitoes faster could save lives Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. That's valuable work, but when health officials are trying to track a disease outbreak, waiting several days can slow their response. Digitomy wants to shorten that process dramatically. Its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured mosquito species the same day. That could help mosquito control teams see where potentially dangerous species are appearing and decide where to concentrate their efforts. This is especially important with Aedes aegypti, the mosquito species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases. Knowing which ones are present can help officials make better decisions. There's one important point to understand. The trap identifies mosquito species capable of carrying disease. It does not automatically prove that a captured mosquito is infected with dengue. Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus. AI mosquito traps could create an early warning system What I find particularly interesting is what happens after the trap identifies a mosquito. Digitomy can send that information to a mapping dashboard, allowing mosquito control teams to see where certain species are appearing. The goal is to give mosquito control teams access to that information the same day, helping them identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. Think about how useful that could be during an outbreak. If several traps begin detecting more Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in one neighborhood, officials could investigate that area and consider targeted mosquito control measures. Instead of waiting for more people to become sick, they could use surveillance data to guide their response. The researchers have already integrated trap information into a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard at mosquitodashboard.org/. That system also incorporates more than half a million citizen science reports. The idea is to combine information from automated traps with observations from people who help track mosquitoes. Digitomy's technology could also complement an existing early warning system developed by Carney for dengue and West Nile virus. Together, these tools could give public health departments a clearer view of mosquito activity across communities. Of course, detecting mosquitoes early doesn't guarantee that an outbreak can be prevented. But faster information could help officials respond sooner, particularly in areas where mosquito control resources are limited. When could communities start using these smart traps? Digitomy has already tested its technology at the University of South Florida and worked with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. The researchers are also preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County, where Florida's dengue outbreak has been especially severe. The startup is working with USF's Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito trap manufacturers. That could allow companies to add the technology to equipment they already produce. Digitomy is working toward commercial availability by licensing its AI technology to established mosquito trap manufacturers. For now, the university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. The company also received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation's Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026. The funding is intended to help accelerate the licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online education platform that would allow mosquito control professionals and the public to practice identifying mosquito species using images and AI-generated feedback. THIRD PERSON DIES AFTER MOSQUITO IS REPORTEDLY TRAPPED ON PLANE TO GERMANY IN 'AIRPORT MALARIA' PHENOMENON Researchers test the AI-powered mosquito trap in a controlled environment as they work to improve mosquito surveillance and help communities respond faster to disease threats. (University of South Florida) What this AI mosquito trap means for you You probably won't be hanging a Digitomy trap in your backyard anytime soon. But that doesn't mean this technology couldn't eventually affect your community. If mosquito control departments adopt smarter surveillance systems, they may be able to identify dangerous mosquito populations sooner and make better decisions about where to intervene. And even though we're heading into November, people living in warmer areas still need to pay attention to mosquito activity. If you're traveling to Florida or another place where mosquitoes remain active, taking precautions is important. For now, the best protection is still fairly simple. Empty standing water from flowerpots and other outdoor containers because mosquitoes can breed in surprisingly small amounts of water. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent when spending time outdoors. Wearing long sleeves and pants can also help reduce exposed skin. We've covered some useful products that can help keep mosquitoes away, including repellents and outdoor gadgets. You can find them in our guide to mosquito and tick repellents at CyberGuy.com Kurt's key takeaways I think this is one of those uses of AI that could make a real difference in people's lives. Most of us see mosquitoes as an annoying part of summer. But Florida's dengue outbreak is a reminder that these tiny insects can cause serious health problems, even late in the year. What interests me about Digitomy is the possibility of giving mosquito control teams information while they still have time to act. The technology looks promising, especially with its reported accuracy in laboratory testing. But I want to see how it performs in real-world conditions before calling it a breakthrough. If it works as researchers hope, communities could have a valuable new tool to help protect people from mosquito-borne diseases. And that's a use of AI I can get behind. Public health authorities across the South Asian nation are facing mounting pressure as hospitals grapple with a continuous influx of patients suffering from the mosquito-borne viral infection, which has severely strained local healthcare infrastructure during the peak transmission period. Check Symptoms Discover more Buy Maps Learn Hindi Explore History Dengue is transmitted primarily by female mosquitoes of the *Aedes* genus, notably *Aedes aegypti*. Following an incubation period ranging from three to 14 days, infected individuals typically experience high fever, severe headaches, vomiting, and muscle and joint pains, often accompanied by a characteristic skin rash. While the majority of cases resolve within a week without long-term complications, a fraction of patients progress to severe dengue—historically referred to as dengue hemorrhagic fever—which is characterized by dangerous drops in blood pressure, plasma leakage, bleeding, and plummeting platelet counts. Check Symptoms The virus exists in four distinct serotypes, complicating both clinical management and epidemiological control. Although recovery from one serotype confers lifelong immunity to that specific strain, subsequent infections involving different serotypes elevate the risk of severe clinical manifestations through a process known as antibody-dependent enhancement. Because early symptoms frequently mimic those of influenza, malaria, or Zika fever, timely laboratory confirmation via blood tests detecting viral RNA or specific antibodies remains crucial for effective patient triage. Discover more Get Health Tips Healthcare infections In the absence of universally curative antiviral treatments, containment strategies rely heavily on vector control, including the reduction of breeding sites through standing water elimination and broad-scale insecticide application. However, shifting monsoon patterns, urbanization trends, and rising global temperatures have expanded the geographic habitat and breeding season of *Aedes* mosquitoes, rendering traditional eradication efforts increasingly difficult in densely populated urban centers like Dhaka. For the broader Indo-Pacific region, escalating vector-borne disease burdens underscore the compounding public health vulnerabilities driven by climate change and rapid urbanization. As tropical and subtropical regions across Asia experience longer monsoon seasons and higher average temperatures, cross-border public health surveillance, joint vector research, and climate-resilient healthcare planning are becoming critical components of regional security and economic stability. This blood-filled mosquito is responsible for transmitting the dengue virus. (Stock photo) The Dominican Republic has the lowest dengue incidence rate among 14 countries and territories in the Americas in a 2026 comparison, with 13.21 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, according to data from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). In epidemiological week 42, the country had accumulated 1,534 dengue cases, a considerably lower number than other nations in the region. Brazil leads the comparison with an incidence rate of 666.67 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, followed by Bolivia (470.26), Panama (273.19), Peru (255.86), and Ecuador (243.90). by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Most People Don’t Know These Ashburn Banks Pay Higher Interest (See the List)Savingspro Click Here Undo In one week, the police have killed eight suspected criminals.The first and only english language online news publication in the Dominican Republic. Your most up to date source for info on the Dominican Republic.Dominican Today Undo The Dominican Republic has a low incidence compared to other countries Other countries with higher rates than the Dominican Republic include Colombia (181.50), Costa Rica (135.62), Guatemala (134.51), El Salvador (108.09), Honduras (94.57), and Mexico (54.98). Among the territories with the lowest incidence are Puerto Rico, with 29.42 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, and Cuba, with 16.03, although both remain above the Dominican Republic. In cumulative cases, Brazil reported 1,406,184; Colombia, 94,618; Peru, 83,430; Mexico, 69,533; and Ecuador, 43,350. Venezuela (13,722 cases), Paraguay (11,348), and Costa Rica (6,654) also surpass the Dominican Republic’s cumulative total, according to data shared by PAHO. The incidence rate allows comparison of the epidemiological situation between countries with different population sizes, unlike absolute figures, which reflect only the number of reported cases. Authorities assure that the situation is under control When consulted by the newspaper HOY, authorities from the Ministry of Public Health explained that the country’s dengue situation remains under control, although cases increased in the provinces of La Romana and La Altagracia over the last four weeks. According to the data provided, 171 cases were reported in epidemiological week 42, but it was not specified whether that amount represents the national total or only the provinces mentioned. Authorities said this increase affected the national figures, but assured that they had already controlled the outbreaks detected in both areas and that the situation in the rest of the national territory remains under control. Dengue fever is decreasing in the Americas At the regional level, PAHO reported 1,914,591 suspected cases of dengue in the Americas in 2026, of which laboratory testing confirmed 605,321. The figure represents a 53% decrease from the same period in 2025 and a 61% decrease from the five-year average, according to the agency. Of the total cases registered, 4,059 were classified as severe dengue and 655 deaths were reported, for a case fatality rate of 0.034%. During epidemiological week 42, 22 countries and territories reported 34,572 new suspected cases. Of these, 96 were classified as severe dengue, and 12 deaths were recorded. supplementary_news.content_title: Florida has the largest continental U.S. dengue fever outbreak in decades — does your snowbird travel insurance cover a mosquito bite?
supplementary_news.content: Melanie Huddart Nov 14, 2026 Share Email Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit Follow us Newsletter Instagram Facebook Tiktok X Youtube Follow us on Google for more Money.ca news Add us on Google Melanie Huddart Nov 14, 2026 Share Email Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit Follow us Newsletter Instagram Facebook Tiktok X Youtube Follow us on Google for more Money.ca news Add us on Google Florida is currently experiencing its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades — just in time for Canadian snowbirds to start planning their winter away in the Sunshine State. The Florida Department of Health, the state’s public health agency, has confirmed 524 locally acquired cases of the virus so far this year, according to its weekly report for Oct. 25 to 31. That’s up from 485 a week earlier. Locally acquired means the virus was spread by mosquitoes in Florida, rather than picked up while travelling abroad. Most cases were reported in Hillsborough County, around Tampa. Melanie Huddart Nov 14, 2026 Share Email Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit Follow us Newsletter Instagram Facebook Tiktok X Youtube Follow us on Google for more Money.ca news Add us on Google Advertisement Thanks for subscribing! The best of Money.ca delivered weekly. By signing up, you accept Money.ca Terms of Use , Subscription Agreement , and Privacy Policy . Most dengue cases are reported as typically mild, but can require a trip to the hospital if symptoms worsen. But if you’re a Canadian in Florida, your provincial health care plan will provide minimal coverage. Whether you are the hook to pay for the rest will depend on what your coverage includes. Thanks for subscribing! The best of Money.ca delivered weekly. By signing up, you accept Money.ca Terms of Use , Subscription Agreement , and Privacy Policy . How serious is Florida’s dengue outbreak? Florida’s outbreak is the largest in the continental U.S. in several decades , according to the Associated Press, the U.S.-based news agency. Data from state health departments and medical journals suggest it marks the most locally acquired cases in a calendar year for any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Florida’s previous worst year was 2023, when just under 200 cases were reported. This year’s count is already more than double that . The outbreak is centralized in one of the most popular destinations for Canadian snowbirds: the Tampa Bay area. As of Oct. 31, Hillsborough County had recorded 407 local cases and Pinellas County 80. Ten other counties have also reported cases, including Orange (Orlando), Miami-Dade and Palm Beach. In September, Florida confirmed its first dengue death of the year: an 80-year-old Tampa woman who passed away on Sept. 4. Dengue is contracted through bites from mosquitoes carrying the virus, not from person-to-person contact. Symptoms include fever, a severe headache and intense joint and muscle pain, which is why dengue is nicknamed “breakbone fever.” Most people have mild symptoms or none at all and recover within one to two weeks, but severe cases can be life-threatening and require hospital care. On Oct. 15, Global Affairs Canada (GAC), the federal department responsible for travel advice, added an outbreak monitoring alert for dengue in Florida to its U.S. travel advice page. The overall risk level for the U.S. didn’t change. It remains at “take normal security precautions,” the lowest of GAC’s four levels . Will your provincial coverage kick in if you get sick in Florida? At best, you might get the very minimal costs covered. Under the Canada Health Act , provinces must pay for emergency care received outside Canada based on what they would have paid for similar services at home. In practice, most provinces pay a flat daily amount that falls short of that standard. The Canadian Snowbird Association (CSA), a non-profit that advocates for Canadian travellers, has lobbied provinces to reimburse at in-province rates. The Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) Out of Country Travellers Program pays up to CA$400 a day for emergency care in an intensive care unit (ICU), coronary care unit or operating room, and up to CA$200 per day for lower levels of inpatient care. For emergency outpatient services, such as an emergency room (ER) visit, it pays up to CA$50 a day or the amount billed, whichever is less. Doctors’ services are reimbursed at Ontario fee-schedule rates. trending now 1 News • 61.1k views Carney: Trump still calls shots on trade 2 News • 53.4k views Whitmer sounds alarm on Canada trade war 3 Managing Money • 32.1k views Canada's $1.1M household net worth trap 4 News • 31.9k views Lutnick revives Canada-U.S. trade talks 5 Investing • 27.8k views Rogers' $25B sports empire stake sale Advertisement Several provinces pay even less, though. Alberta , Saskatchewan and Quebec cap emergency inpatient care at CA$100 a day, while British Columbia pays CA$75 a day . These fixed amounts cover only a sliver of U.S. hospital bills. B.C.’s Ministry of Health warns that a day in a U.S. hospital often costs more than US$1,000 and can reach US$10,000 in intensive care. In Florida, hospitals spent an average of US$2,487 to US$3,382 per adjusted inpatient day in 2024, depending on the type of hospital, according to KFF, a U.S. non-profit health policy research organization. That’s what it costs hospitals to provide care, not what they bill patients. Physician fees, tests and ambulance rides come on top, so even a short hospital stay can add up quickly. Will your travel insurance cover dengue? In most cases, a sudden illness like dengue falls under the emergency medical portion of your travel insurance policy. But some details in the fine print can determine whether your claim is covered. Travel advisories Typically, Canadian insurance policies will state limits or exclusions based on Ottawa’s warnings against non-essential travel, or all travel to specific destinations. While the U.S. is well below an advisory of this level, and the dengue flag shouldn’t be enough to trigger a blanket exclusion, be vigilant in understanding how your policy treats a specific health warning — the wording matters most. Pre-existing health conditions Snowbirds usually represent an older demographic, and are more likely to have health conditions. If dengue further complicates an existing condition, your insurer will examine your medical history against your medical questionnaire. If you withheld a medical condition on your questionnaire, or if your condition or medication changed during your policy’s stability period — the window before departure when a pre-existing condition must stay unchanged to be covered — you could be denied coverage for claims related to that condition. Trip duration Many snowbird insurance policies cap the number of days you can spend outside of Canada. If your stay runs past that limit, you could be uninsured over those extra days. The Travel Health Insurance Association of Canada (THIA), which represents the country’s travel insurance industry, has long urged travellers to make sure they’re fully covered. “With U.S. medical costs among the highest in the world, proper coverage is non-negotiable,” THIA executive director Will McAleer said when the association released its 2025 winter travel survey . Read more: 3 essential money moves to make once you’ve saved $50,000 What can you do to protect yourself? Florida’s dengue outbreak doesn’t mean cancelling your winter travel plans altogether. But it’s a good reminder to carefully review your coverage, while limiting your exposure to mosquitoes. Buy insurance coverage before you take off. Only relying on your provincial plan is risky. Get travel medical insurance to cover your entire time away Answer the medical questionnaire carefully and honestly. List every condition, name every medication and make your insurer aware of any changes before you leave — even minor ones Ask about travel advisories. Ask your broker or insurer how your policy applies if Canada’s cross-border travel advice changes while you’re away Check your employer or retiree group benefits. Some plans include out-of-country coverage, but it may be more restrictive than a snowbird policy Know who to call in an emergency. Save your insurer’s 24-hour emergency assistance number in your phone. Many policies require you to call before receiving treatment, or within 24 to 48 hours of an emergency, and to follow the advice to keep your coverage Prevent mosquito bites. Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants, empty standing water around your property and limit your time outdoors — dengue-carrying mosquitoes can bite at any time of day, not just at dusk. Watch for symptoms. If you’re suddenly hit with a fever, severe headache or body aches, see a doctor immediately.
